Public Works-Kenogami public building, $31,000.

What is this for? Has
the minister some explanation? We do not know anything about this.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
This amount of $31,000 is required
for the construction of a public building in the town of Kenogami for postal purposes on a site situated at the corner of King George avenue and Ste. Famile street, purchased from J. O. Lacroix for the sum of $5,800.

What is the population and the amount of business done by the post office there?
. Mr. ELLIOTT:	The population in 1921
was 2,557, and is now somewhere around 3,000, I understand.
What is the revenue?
The revenue is $7,262.45.

This is just another of
these cases where, with a gross revenue of $7,000 it is proposed to spend $31,000 on a new building; our net revenue from that post office for the next ten years will go into that building. Is the building under construction, or has it been started?

In connection with this proposed post office I may say that the town of Kenogami is very close to Jonquiere, where Price Brothers have their large paper mill, and it is also very close to the large aluminum plant which is being built. Within the last year the population of Kenogami has doubled; there are now 5,000 people in that town with no postal accommodation whatever. The post office to-day is located in a store.

Cannot the government
rent premises there?

Not in any place that we
know of. It is a new village and even the population can hardly find the requisite lodging because of the tremendous development produced by the operations of the aluminum company and the paper mills at Kenogami.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is where Price
Brothers have their big plant.
What is the explanation of the high cost of the lot? The sum of $5,800 seems to be a very high price for a lot in that village.

I assume it is the same
reason that brings about high prices wherever a town seems to be booming. The population has doubled there within the last five years, and business seems to be very active. Not only have sites increased very greatly in value but buildings also.
When was this lot purchased?

The lot was purchased
on the 21st October, 1925.

Was it purchased by
private treaty or by public competition? Were tenders called for? I notice the purchase was made six weeks before the election. From whom was it purchased?
It was purchased from Mr J. O. Lacroix.
What officer of the government did the purchasing, or how was it done?

I assume the lot was
purchased in the usual way. An officer of the department is usually sent down and looks over the lot. I may say to my hon. friend very frankly that my notes do not indicate what steps were taken towards purchasing it, but I assume it was done in the manner indicated.

Can the minister tell
me the name of the officer in the department? There are some good officers and some
that are not good ones.

They are nearly all good
in the department.
Oh, no, they are not.

Did you buy
the land down there by the acre or by the foot? Tell us what the assessment is and we will find out what the value should be.
This is a comer lot and was bought by the foot two years ago, but it could not be purchased to-day for the price the government paid.

How many
feet are there in the lot? You have not furnished the information asked for yet.
The approximate dimensions are 75 by 125 feet. It is at the intersection of two important streets. It is the finest site in Kenogami being right in the very centre of the town.

All I can
say about it is that the whole business looks a little funny. I am not in a position to criticize the transaction in detail. If I had all the information-and I am sure some of the hon. members who live in the district must have-it might appear to me to be all right. Let me say, however, in closing this this matter as far as I am concerned at the moment, that I hope that next session when I come forward and ask for a post office building in a town of this size, or larger, and with far greater prospects of development than this-
Oh, oh.
Yes-
You had better go and see what is taking place there.
-I will not be faced with the difficulties that I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no Kenogami in your district.
Drumheller is likely to develop to as great an extent as Kenogami if not greater.

No doubt Drumheller is a progressive place and a fine town but my hon. friend should have more information when he talks of a subject like this. The statement of the Minister of Justice as to my ignorance of conditions there would come with better grace from him if the minister handling the subject knew more about it.

Item agreed to.
Limoilou-public building, $70,000.

Will the minister give
us pretty full information as to this item? It is a very big vote for a public building.
Tenders have been let, and we are asking for $50,000 instead of last year's vote of $70,000.

Would the minister be
good enough to speak up?

I will do the best I can and try to make my hon. friend hear. I am going to ask for $50,000 instead of $70,000. If one of my colleagues will make the motion we will have that change made. This amount of $50,000 is required for the erection of a public building on a site situated on La Canadierre road in the town of Limoilou. The proposed building will be a two storey stone structure 52 feet wide by 40 feet deep with a one storey annex at the rear 39 feet wide by 14 feet 6 inches deep. The building will provide accommodation for the postal service on the ground floor and will have offices and caretaker's quarters on the second floor.
What is the population?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

What is the explanation of this item?

This amount of $25,000 is required for the fitting up of the old city hall building at Maisonneuve, which was purchased in 1926-27 from the municipal authorities for postal purposes. The purchase price of the building was $100,000, and the fitting up is estimated to cost $25,000.

When was the building
purchased?
During the past year some time.
And what is the population of Maisonneuve?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is part of the city of Montreal.

$100,000?

That was the purchase
price.
Last year there seems to have been a vote of $50,000 and this year we are asked to vote $25,000. How did we pay for the building?

That $50,000 I think is
wrong. I have a note here which says that the amount of $50,000 in the 1926-27 column in the printed book was inserted by the Finance department. It is wrong; the correct amount is $125,000.
$100,000 for last year and $25,000 for this year?

Item agreed to.
Quebec Citadel-Governor General's quarters -additions, alterations and improvements, $100,000.
Explain.

This vote is required for
the remodelling of the Governor General's quarters in the Quebec citadel. The improvements embrace works of a miscellaneous character consisting of the remodelling and renovating of the quarters and the erection of a permanent addition for servants' quarters, kitchen and so forth. The work, it is estimated, will cost approximately $100,000. This was formerly the residence during part of the year of the Governor General, but the premises have fallen into disrepair to such an extent that the improvements will require the amount specified here, if the place is to be made habitable. It is Their Excellencies' desire to visit Quebec city twice a year.
Would it be possible to secure a suite at the Chateau in Quebec for the use of Their Excellencies, and so avoid this expenditure?

I have no doubt it would be possible to get a suite there, but I can assure my hon. friend that the item has not been inserted in the estimates without the most careful canvass of the whole situation
Even if satisfactory quarters could be obtained elsewhere for the accommodation of Their Excellencies, the government are of the opinion that we should not abandon this old historic building, a part of which was built over a hundred years ago. It is perhaps one of the most valuable historic monuments that exist on the American continent to-day, and is of interest not only to Canadians but generally.

I agree with the minister in regard to this vote. I think we ought to preserve this historic monument of past days for it is something in which every citizen of Canada should take a just pride. I have not visited the citadel since the Duke of Devonshire was here as Governor General, and even at that time the whole premises were sadly out of repair. If nothing has been done in the intervening years the place must be in a very dilapidated condition today. Possibly the amount asked for, $100,000, is large, but having regard to the fact that this is one of the outstanding historic sites in Canada I believe that the people of the country desire to have it maintained in a condition befitting our wealth and consequence in this land. While I am disposed' to criticize much of the outlay proposed in these estimates, while I do oppose political expenditures throughout the country on post offices and other buildings for which there is no need at the present time, I am inclined to commend this vote, and I hope that the money we are now granting will place the Quebec citadel in proper shape, not only for the comfort of Their Excellencies, but also as a monument in which the Dominion at large is interested.

I have no desire to criticize any amount the government may spend1 to maintain historic buildings in Quebec or anywhere else in Canada. May I point out, however, that we have had no explanation so far as to how much money is going to be spent on the kitchen and how much will be devoted to the restoration of the historic portion of the premises. It is just possible that an inadequate proportion of the vote will be spent for the purpose indicated by the leader of the opposition, and in that case the grant will be altogether contrary to the views he has expressed. The minister might tell us how the $100,000 is to be apportioned.

I am unable to give very
definite details. The architect has been over the building but I may frankly tell my hon. friend that at this time of year it is quite difficult to estimate what it will cost to preserve a considerable portion of the existing

structure. This vote is merely an estimate. The full amount will, however, be required and before the department is able to put the premises in that permanent shape which we desire, I rather think the amount will be exceeded. An attempt is being made to render the place habitable, as it is not now, both for winter and summer. Furthermore, a good deal of furnishing will be required as well as inside fittings. This is the estimate which the architect, after a careful survey of the whole place, was able to submit to us.

How long is it intended
that the citadel will be occupied by Their Excellencies?

Of course, that depends
upon the occupant. I should like to be able to give my hon. friend more information in regard to the matter, but I really cannot say how long they intend to keep up the old traditions in regard to retaining their headquarters at the citadel for a portion of the year.
May I ask if the battlements, the walls, of the old citadel and everything connected with it are under the jurisdiction of my hon. friend's department?

The fortifications are
under the Department of National Defence. I can give my hon. friend an exact description of the portion under Public Works, which is the part occupied for residential purposes.

In case I may not be
here when the National Defence estimates come before the House, I may say that I passed in front of the citadel last fall, and I observed that the walls and battlements were in a very bad state. Certainly there is urgent need of works and repairs for the preservation of that historic monument-I think much more urgent from that point of view than the object of the present item; I do not mean from the other point of view presented by the minister. The matter of the preservation of the monument has been neglected for some years past. I have observed, for example, in the moat surrounding the citadel and connected with the entrance to the internal courts, the wall is partly coming down and work is urgently required there.

I quite agree with what has been said by my hon. friend from Labelle. For the past seven or eight years, nearly every session, I have had a resolution on the order paper asking that the ancient walls and fortifications of Quebec be transferred from

the Department of National Defence, in view of the fact that they are no longer useful for military purposes, to some historic commission, preferably to the National Battlefields Commission. When the hon. leader of the opposition was Minister of National Defence he received the resolution with grea^ cordiality and took steps to transfer i portion of the 'ancient walls o<f the city of Quebec. The portion leading from Mountain hill over to Palais hill I think has been transferred in part to the city of Quebec. At the present time negotiations have been undertaken between the Minister of Justice and the Minister of National Defence, the mayor of Quebec, I think also Mr. Turgeon, speaker of the legislative council, and Sir George Garneau, with a view to having the three authorities, federal, provincial and municipal take the walls out of the control of the Department of National Defence, where they should not be, and preserve that historic monument for the future. With regard to this particular vote, in so far as it will help to build up the walls near where the Governor General's quarters are, it has my hearty support and endorsement. In order that the House may know that there is nothing political in this, I may say that the citadel is situated in my constituency, and I never knew until the estimates came down that there was any question of having a vote to repair the Governor General's quarters. I have made no representations to the Minister of National Defence or any minister with reference to this matter, but I may say that the repairs had been asked for by His Excellency, Lord Byng, and by other Governors General. Moreover it is, I understand, the intention of the government and of Their Excellencies to receive the Prince of Wales at the Quebec citadel next summer when he comes to Canada, and it is only fitting that the quarters should be put into proper repair and made fit to receive the prince.

Item agreed to.
Quebec-Savard Park hospital-repairs and alterations, $5,000.
What hospital is this?

Quebec Park hospital.
This is for general repairs and improvements to the park hospital as requested by the deputy minister.

A marine hospital or a
Department of Soldier's Civil Re-establishment. hospital?

Supply-Public Works-Quebec
It is one of the quarantine hospitals of the Health department.

Item agreed to.
St. Jacques L'Achigan-public building, $21,-
000.
Is this for a postal building? I should like to know the revenue of the post office and the population of the place.

The annual revenue is
$2,689, and the population is around 1,500.
I notice this is a revote of $16,000. Is it a new building entirely, or simply an addition to the old building?

It is a new building now
under contract. It is a revote.
Do public buildings mentioned in the estimates include post offices?
If it is merely a post office it is so described. If it is a building including post office, customs and armoury, it is then called a public building.

The minister has given
the revenue from the post office, I understand, which has no bearing-
The postal revenue is supposed to have some relation to the business being done in a particular community.

Besides the post office there is an excise office, there are five manufacturers of tobacco, and the revenue in 1920 was $18,000. I have not the latest revenue figures, but the offices are used for both post office and excise purposes.

I should like to ask what
is the policy of the department regarding the construction of post offices. The minister has given as a reason for the construction of this building the fact that the place has a population of 1,500, I think he said, and a revenue of $2,600. I think I could find quite a few places in my riding that I would like to bring to his attention, if that is to be the guiding consideration. Surely there must be some special reason for putting up a building in this place. If not, we may as well all get in on this. I have not made a request for the last ten or twelve years for an item of public expenditure in my riding outside of the town of Collingwood, which is an important harbour and has been for years and years, because I have understood right. along that we were supposed to cut down and stop that sort of thing altogether. I have not heard a solitary reason advanced in this House for the construction of this building, or for that matter for the construction of buildings in

a number of other places for which votes have gone through. I have no reference to the last item. If there is no other reason than a population of 1,500 and a revenue of $2,600, I would ask the minister if I come along with a proposal or two for public buildings in Simcoe county, in villages with a population of 1,500 and a revenue of $2,600, will he grant my request as well as the requests of other members of this House who have a similar situation in their ridings? If not, why is this item in here? Why is a building put up here and not elsewhere?

If my hon. friend comes
with any request it will be very carefully considered, there is no doubt about that; and if the treasury had to depend for its protection on my generosity, it would not be as nearly as well protected as now when I have to get past the treasury board and council. But I think my hon. friend's question is a fair one in view of what is taking place. It is a matter to which I have personally given very serious thought. The policy of this government, as I stated the other evening, is not to construct public buildings for post offices or any other service except where they are very urgently needed. Various considerations enter into the question. Take the case of the public building that was being considered a short time ago at Kenogami, where the growth has been very rapid and it is impossible to get a store or other suitable building in a place of that kind. Take certain ridings, perhaps like my hon. friend's, which have received no public expenditure of any kind for a number of years, and there are a great many rural ridings in that category. Somebody asked, Why construct a public building in a place where the population is only so much and the revenue is only $1,500 or something of that kind? I would ask hon. members to consider the question in relation to a riding where there are no other public works, such as harbours, docks or anything of that nature, and where as a matter of absolute necessity, there has been no public expenditure perhaps for years, because in recent times there has been very little expenditure on buildings. The department is only constructing public buildings in places where the present facilities are inadequate, where the public are not getting the service to which they are entitled, where it is considered in the public interest to construct those buildings and where such construction does not involve a departure from a policy of rigid economy.

The minister has not given us any special reason for this at all. He has only emphasized what I have tried to urge,

Supply-Public Works-Quebec
that it has been the desire to economize, and that if there is going to be any expenditure it should be in ridings which have not had much public expenditure, and so on. But I have not heard a word to show that there is any special reason for the construction of this building. There may not be a post office there now, but surely one can be rented. I have in mind no end of places within a radius of one hundred miles of my own town where there is identically the same situation, but they are not getting anything. Let us hear from the minister why an exception is being made of this place. I know nothing about it personally, and I am not singling it out for attack; I simply want to know what is the general policy, and I want to be given some reason why this should be done in this case. If there is no special reason, I want the minister to give us all an invitation to pester him with applications in the future. He says that we may trust to his generosity. Well, I would like to feel that I could do that, and if he really means that as an invitation I shall be round to see him in the next year or two because I have two or three places already in mind. Let us see if we cannot get some reason why this building should be constructed.

My hon. friend knows
perfectly well that any visit from him would not be considered by anybody as pestering; I know7 my hon. friend too well for that. But so far as throwing out a wholesale invitation for everybody to solicit public buildings is concerned, I do not intend to do that, because I am endeavouring to carry out the policy that my hon. friend has indicated he i3 in favour of, of constructing public buildings only where they are urgently needed, and this particular building is only being constructed because there is no other building there that will afford adequate accommodation. The contract has been let arid the building is under way.

I would just like to say
to the minister that he is, consciously or unconsciously, throwing out the very invitation which he says he does not wish to give. I will admit that up to this year there has been a policy on the part of all governments since the war not to construct public buildings. I pointed out the other evening that there were some eighty or ninety places where sites had been purchased as far back as 1910 or 1911, when Canada did not owe two and a half billion dollars, with the intention of putting up public buildings. I gave Fort Frances as an instance. A site was bought there in 1910 or 1911, and there are from
[Mr. Boys.l
seventy-five to ninety other places where sites have been bought. Up to this present year the government, and our previous government, and the government before that, have lived up to the policy of not putting up buildings that were not absolutely necessary, but certainly this year when one looks through the estimates, one cannot fail to see that that policy has been absolutely departed from. I notice a number of public buildings for Ontario and Quebec, and we had a vote the other evening for a public building in Kensington, Prince Edward Island. I certainly submit to the minister that he is giving us all an invitation, by this departure from what has been the policy, to press for public buildings in various parts of the country, and I again draw to his attention the case of Fort Frances, which is not now in my constituency, but in the constituency of the present Minister of Labour, and which I pressed for a long time until I saw that the policy of both governments, ours and the previous government, was against public buildings of that kind. I think the minister would be well advised either to cut out a number of these items, or to make up his mind that he is certainly going to be pressed by members from all over the country for public buildings which are just as much needed as this one. Fort Frances, for instance, has a population of about four thousand. It is a prosperous, progressive, go-ahead little town with not a public building. They are right on the border, and they require not only a post office, but a customs office and an immigration office. Up until very recently they were in a rented office-

If my hon. friend will
permit me, we have recently been able to get very satisfactory and commodious quarters in the Masonic temple at Fort Frances, and perhaps that is the reason why a new building is not being asked for there. If that building had not been available we would have been forced to erect a building as in these other cases.

I know the Masonic building and I do not agree that it offers very commodious post office quarters for a town of the size of Fort Frances, but it is much better than the former accommodation. However, the point I make is that when I was the member for Fort Frances I absolutely refused pressing for a building for that town because it was the policy of the then government and of its predecessor not to erect public buildings owing to the then state of the national finances. But now apparently the government is departing from that

Supply-Public Works-Quebec
policy, and I fear the minister is laying himself open to pressure from all sections of the country for public buildings. During the last election I declared on the hustings at practically every place where I spoke that the government was making a mistake in departing from the policy of the two or three administrations of the past-the policy of renting accommodation such as we were doing in Fort Frances. This afternoon we have passed two or three items for public buildings, and while it is true that at Kenogami the aluminum plant is causing a rapid development of the town, that is all the more reason, I submit, why we should have rented a building temporarily so that we may be in a better position later on to judge of the ultimate requirements of the locality.

My hon. friend must be
perfectly well aware that where a town has doubled its population in five years you cannot rent buildings.

That is a very lame explanation. Does the minister mean to tell me that in such a progressive community there are no enterprising people who would not gladly put up a temporary building to rent to the postal department?
Why should not the government put up its own temporary building?

I have no objection if it
is to be the policy of the government. This will only be a temporary building anyhow. But I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the government is making a mistake in departing from the policy of not putting up public buildings where suitable accommodation can be rented, and I certainly believe the minister as a result will soon find himself so importuned by requests for public buildings at one point and another throughout the Dominion that he will wish himself back in the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment.

Where there are no
troubles!
There are some, I admit.

Mr. Chairman, I would
direct the attention of the minister to another angle of this situation. I notice that the total expenditure for the province of Quebec this year is 1635,027, while last year it was only $327,050. We are spending pretty nearly double in that province this year. Naturally, we come to the conclusion that the rest of the Dominion is entitled to an increased expenditure in the same ratio. In contrast to what is being done for Quebec, I turn to my own
province of British Columbia, where I find that last year the expenditure on public works was $216,760, and this year it is $243,262-a slight increase, but not at all in proportion to the increased expenditure in Quebec. I submit in all seriousness that the demand for public buildings in British Columbia is equally as imperative as in Quebec. It is quite true that the latter province is going ahead at a very nice rate, but it is also true that important developments are taking place in my province. It seems to me if that is the excuse for the increased expenditure in Quebec, British Columbia should have been given more consideration.

Perhaps, Mr. Chairman,
political developments in the province of Quebec were more satisfactory than in my hon. friend's province.

The criticism of my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) is perfectly sound. There is no need whatever for these new buildings to-day. He suggests a temporary structure, but there is no need even for that. Any store in that locality could very well provide accommodation for a branch post office, at a cost of practically nothing. In my riding we have several branch post offices, and I will guarantee that every one of them does more business than is transacted in any of these towns of 30,000 population. So it is a waste of money to buy votes in these little burgs. I should like to ask if any other buildings are required in the province of Quebec? Are you sure that you do not need a new city hall or an old one repaired?
My hon. friend knows that that is a municipal responsibility.

I know, but
several of these items appear to me to be municipal too. Is it the intention of the minister of erect all new buildings required in the province of Quebec as well as public buildings belonging strictly to the federal government?
Why not?

That is what
you are getting.

Mr. Chairman, for
a couple of days I have been waiting to hear the minister give the reasons underlying these expenditures on public buildings. Revenue apparently has nothing to do with the expenditure.
Population.

No.

The good looks of the member.
The only requirement seems to be a beautiful surrounding country. Will the minister state what factors enter into the granting of these public buildings?

My hon. friend will see
that in Quebec the greater proportion of expenditure is in Conservative ridings.

Two wrongs
don't make a right. If my party did wrong, that is no reason why yours should do wrong too.

It answers my hon.
friend's argument absolutely. My hon. friend from Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) referred to what he termed the increased expenditure for public buildings in Quebec over that voted last year, but he has overlooked the fact that the total of $635,027 includes $100,000 for the Quebec citadel, $50,000 for a postal station in Outremont and $50,000 for reorganization of the Montreal general post office. Those three items make up the difference between last year's and this year's expenditure. With regard to the buildings in Haileybury destroyed by fire and which are being rebuilt, I wish to inform the House that in October, 1922, a fire swept a great part of the country up there and the town of Haileybury was wiped out. The people of Haileybury had been using the armouries at different times for public meetings of various kinds during the preceding summer, and they had put insurance upon the armouries to the amount of 833,500, to protect the Department of Public Works against fire loss if the building should be burned while in use by them. It was a great conflagration which wiped out the homes of many of the farmers for miles around and destroyed nearly the whole town of Haileybury, burning the armouries. This insurance of $33,500 was placed by the people of Haileybury on the building at that time. After that the town of Haileybury commenced to build up again, and it has been almost restored to the position it was in before the fire of 1922. At different times after 1922 the people of Haileybury conferred with the government in Ottawa for the purpose of having the armouries rebuilt and having the $33,500 expended as quickly as possible. They wanted the armouries built in preference to any other public building which the government might erect. There were many reasons for that. Thousands of our boys in the north country formed a corps for the first time in the armouries building in Haileybury and there was a sentimental reason for desiring to see the armouries rebuilt. Since war time they had been using the armouries for public meetings and other purposes for the benefit of the community. When the armouries are completed the people are willing to do their part in regard to repairs and insurance if the department so requires. We sincerely hope that there may never come another occasion when the building will be needed for the purpose for which it was utilized during the war years, but if the necessity should arise I can assure the House that the building will
be used just as extensively to help forward the nation's war efforts. As I say, the old building was insured for $33,500 by the people of Haileybury. This money was collected by the department and expended on the new armouries, so up to the present the building has not cost the government one dollar. In addition to that, the government got the benefit of the interest on the money during the three years before they expended it. I am confident that this will be a very useful building when completed not only for use as armouries but also for holding public meetings, and the people are ^lad indeed that this accommodation will soon be available to them.

Sites for these projected buildings were purchased by the government some time ago, and I would ask the Minister of Militia to see that work in connection with the armouries is proceeded with.

I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that this is not a case where I can even talk about favourable consideration just now, and we might as well be frank about it. The situation in regard to armouries has been very forcibly brought to my attention during the short time that I have been in the Department of National Defence, and I intend to have a survey made with a view to seeing if any better accommodation can be provided in certain cases, but I am afraid I cannot hold out very much hope of constructing new armouries just now. Propositions have come to me from various parts of the Dominion offering capital and sites of considerable value in an endeavour to induce the department to forward these capital expenditures. As far as we possibly can we are providing accommodation for training purposes. As the hon. member is aware, many of our armoury buildings were erected during the war. I am sorry that I cannot hold out any hope of further capital expenditure at the moment.

Item agreed to.
Ottawa departmental buildings-fittings, etc., $60,000. .

Where is that for, may
I ask? Is it for any particular building?

That is for all the
buildings in Ottawa.

Item agreed to.
Public Works-Ottawa-greenhouse, $27,000.

I would like
to ask what particular use we have for a greenhouse except to provide flowers for the House of Commons and the Senate? Why should we spend $27,000 for that?
This amount is to provide for the construction of a greenhouse and potting shed either in Major Hill park or on parliament hill, to replace the greenhouse now looated in Major Hill park.

What is to be
the size of the proposed building?
The estimated cost is

The building
we have now and which has served the purpose for years seems to have been large enough up to the present time. I will admit that the present building is dilapidated and that we require a new one, but if the new one were of the same size it would be sufficient for all our business unless it is to be used commercially.

The building we are
replacing is dilapidated, out of repair and practically falling down, and this estimate is for that replacement.

I assume the
present building to be about 20 by 80; I do not think it is any larger, and from what I know about greenhouses a building of that kind can be constructed and equipped with a good water heating plant for less than $5,000. Why is $27,000 required?

All I can say to my hon.
friend is that this is the architect's estimate. It is proposed to construct a greenhouse for Major Hill park to replace the present greenhouse which is beyond repair, as the woodwork has become so badly decayed that to renew it would practically mean rebuilding the superstructure. This is a revote.

Is the structure to be
gothic or romanesque?

I object to
putting $27,000 into a greenhouse; it is too much for the purpose intended, and there is no need for it at all. I would suggest that the amount be reduced to $10,000, which would provide twice the amount necessary, and I make that motion, Mr. Chairman.

I might say in that
regard that on account of the location and the fact that at is here in the capital city, $10,000 would not be very much money for the construction of such a building. The amount placed in the estimate is considered by the architect to be sufficient to no more than replace the present building, so that I hope my hon. friend will reconsider his motion.

I am quite well satisfied that there is not need for such an

Supply-Public Works-Manitoba
amount for that purpose. I know that you can build a modem steel frame greenhouse with a first-class hot water heating plant, larger than the present building, for $10,000.
Amendment negatived.

Item agreed to.
Ottawa-towards purchase of building for government workshops, $13,300.

May we
have an explanation from the minister on this item? Where are these workshops?

This is the fifth payment
on the purchase of the property.

Is that the
property on George street?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Rockland-public building, $25,000.

I have not been very
long in Ottawa, but I would like to refer the minister to the ramshackle old building in which the Bureau of Statistics is located. The floors in that building are like the waves of the ocean, and I would like to know if there is to be an appropriation for a new building or if something can be done to make that building more suitable for the purposes for which it is used. If a fire should come along all those valuable records would be lost. Is there to be any provision made for that in the near future?

I might say that the building referred to is one of many in Ottawa entirely out of repair and unsuitable for the purposes for which they are used. It is the intention of the department to start upon a program of construction of departmental buildings as rapidly as the funds can be obtained; it is intended to make a start this year.

May I suggest that that
is one of the most dangerous fire traps I have ever seen, and that such valuable documents should be transferred to some stone building which would be more fire-proof.
Will the minister give us some explanation of this item for a public building in Rockland?

This amount is to provide for the purchase of a site and for the construction iof a public building in the
town of Rockland. It is proposed to pay $2,000 for a site; $18,000 for the building; $2,500 for fittings, lock boxes, et cetera; $1,500 for grading and sidewalks and $1,000 for contingencies.

Who has requested this
building? Who has made the demand?

I have. Surely my hon.
friend is not so badly informed as not to know where Rockland is. It is one of the principal towns on the provincial highway between Ottawa and Montreal and one of the most flourishing towns we have in the county of Russell. The population is close to 5,000, and I think Rockland amply deserves a post office.

Item agreed to.
Toronto-postal station A, mechanical equipment, $50,000.
Is this a political vote?
I can assure my hon. friend that none of these are political votes.

Item agreed to.
Manitoba-Dominion public buildings-improvements, repairs, etc., $35,000.
Would the minister tell me if the public building at Morden is included in the list of repairs referred to here?
-I may say to my hon. friend that this is a general vote for the whole of the province, and I assume that if the needs at Morden are as urgent as at some other places they will receive consideration.
I understand then that the details of this expenditure are not decided upon?
No.

Item agreed to.
Winnipeg-grain inspection building, $13,000.
Is it proposed to include in the estimates any vote for the testing laboratory at Winnipeg?
That is under the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I cannot say offhand what, the intentions are in that regard.

Item agreed to.
Saskatchewan-Dominion public buildings- improvements, repairs, etc., $17,000.

I wish to say a word about
the needs of the town of Biggar in Saskatchewan. Provision has been made for new public
Supply-Public

Works-Saskatchewan
buildings in a number of places where it is claimed conditions demand it. But it seems almost impossible to get decent post office accommodation in the town of Biggar. The present post office is located in a shack between a Chinese laundry and a pool room, and the fire hazard is tremendous. Biggar is a thriving place in Saskatchewan, a divisional point on the Canadian National railway, and the Canadian Pacific passes it at a distance of one mile. Railways also go north and south from Biggar, and it is a growing place. The present population is about 2,500, and the revenue from the post office last year was $10,054. Seeing that votes for public buildings in other places have already been adopted, some of which are not nearly as urgent as in the case of Biggar, and considering the needs of the town, I would ask particularly that the government place a sufficient amount in the supplementary estimates to give Biggar a suitable public building.

I happen to know the
town of Biggar very well, and I take it from what the hon. gentleman says that he is in favour of the erection of a public building there. In that respect he disagrees with some other hon. members who do not think public buildings should be erected anywhere. The case of Biggar is very deserving no doubt and will receive consideration when more urgent cases have been provided for. I will be very glad to give the matter the best consideration I can.

Does the minister not think that this is one of the most urgent cases? The business done there exceeds that of -other places some of them only one-fifth the size and earning less than one-third the revenue of Biggar, and yet those places have been voted public buildings. I think the needs of Biggar should receive immediate consideration.

Item agreed to.
Moose Jaw-public buildings-improvements and repairs, $3,500.

I know one cannot ask the minister to increase this item but I should like to say that while this post office may not show as big a revenue as other post offices I think it does a lot more work than any other post office in the province of Saskatchewan seeing that the mails for a great many branch lines are sorted there, and it is the transfer office for practically all the United States mails that come into that country. I do not believe the present vote will cover the improvements and repairs that 
should be made in that office, and I want tc ask the minister if he will not introduce intc the next estimates brought down a sufficien* amount of money to take care of all those repairs and improvements?

Item agreed to.
Regina public building-addition to site, $150,000.
I should like to ask what the dimensions of this site are and the other details concerning it.

The first question from
that side of the House to-day.

This amount of $150,000 is required for the purchase of property having a frontage of 50 feet on Scarth street, south of and adjoining the post office property, as a means of extending the post office building for the purpose of centralizing all the government offices in the city of Regina in one building.	.
Do I understand the minister to say that they are paying $3,000 a foot for property in Regina?
Perhaps my hon. friend will permit me-

Could the Minister of
Railways give us some more accurate information?

The question of post
office accommodation in Regina is not one of local patronage in any sense.
No, we quite understand that.

Regina is the fifth largest revenue office in the Dominion. It will I know astonish some hon. members when I say that in the middle west we have an office which is the fifth largest revenue producer, yielding as it did $802,000 of revenue last year.
I thought Moose Jaw was larger.

It does more
work.

I am not going to discuss the amount of work done. Usually the amount of money received has some relationship to the amount of work done, but I do not propose to quarrel with my hon. friends from Moose Jaw and Saskatoon.

This is the most costly; that is the point.

Supply-Public Works-Saskatchewan

Yes. Past governments
have on various occasions attempted to remedy the undesirable situation that has existed there for a number of years, and the government of which my hon. friends opposite were members bought a site, not adjacent to the post office at all, intending to use it for customs purposes. This site was acquired a number of years ago. The great problem in that city with regard to the post office is lack of ground floor space, and consequently the erection of a building elsewhere would not solve the post office difficulty. Naturally, as representing, the city, I should prefer to ask for another public building to house the various Dominion offices there, but I recognize that such a building would not meet the situation in regard to ground floor space and the mechanical appliances necessary to handle the great volume of business now being done. Several years ago a small building across the alley was purchased to give additional space. It is connected by an overhead passageway with the main post office, but it does not in any sense contribute to the solution of the main problem, which is one of ground floor space. There was some discussion a year ago with regard to the purchase of fifty feet immediately south of the post office, and some negotiations were entered into between the Department of Public Works and the owners of the property. The price asked Was, however, deemed too high and the provision being made here is to permit expropriation proceedings to be taken. That is the method the department proposes to pursue in connection with the acquisition of this property.

Will the expropriation
proceedings be taken in the Exchequer court?

Yes. I may say frankly that the post office in Regina is located in a situation where, to add to it, would involve the purchasing of some of the most highly priced property in the city, nad it is a question to determine whether we can better deal with this very awkward problem by erecting somewhere else an entirely new public building or by adding to the present post office. Officers of the department, more particularly the officers of the Post Office Department, can see no solution to the post office problem in Regina unless the present floor space is extended; and the property which it is proposed to expropriate consists of a fifty-foot frontage, one hundred and twenty-five feet in depth, I believe.
With buildings?

There is a large restaurant on the property now, a single storey building. Frankly, my own opinion is that the expropriation should have been made many years ago, when of course the property could have been acquired at a lower price. Had that been done we should not be in our present situation. I think I am right in saying-the Minister of Public Works can correct me if I am wrong-that it is proposed to dispose of the small building to which I referred a little while ago, and this will in a measure offset the expenditure here asked for. Once the site is acquired, however, it will be necessary to come back to parliament for enough money to erect the addition to the post office, which is very urgently required.
What is the population of Regina?

About 40,000. The postal revenue of the city is $802,000, and Regina is unique among places in its revenue class in that this is the only post office building in the city which is government owned. All the sub-stations are merely rented premises.

Do you expect to get
any return from the building which is to be scrapped?

I cannot say what its
salvage value would be, but there will be a revenue from the sale of the small building now owned by the government. It is a valuable property, but, as I say, it is across an alley from the present post office. Facing as it does, however, on one of the main streets in the city I think probably it will fetch a good price, although it is only twenty-five feet in width.

I am not
objecting to this vote because I happen to know the situation, and these western cities have grown to such an extent that it is necessary to augment their post office facilities. I would point out, however, that in the city I represent, situate in the centre of the constituency, we have, unlike Regina, a very inferior building. The building in Regina, while not large enough, is a good structure. I would urge upon the government the importance of providing proper post office accommodation in the city of Saskatoon. We have there a site which is a water hole, about 140 feet by 140, and there is a good deal of complaint in the city about its condition. The authorities paid $135,000 for the site, which is one of the legacies bequeathed us by the Tories. It was purchased several blocks away from the centre of the city and
1130	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-Saskatchewan
is not at all suitable for a post office. We feel that the time has come when we should have a new public building in Saskatoon, and I am in hopes that in the supplementary estimates a sufficient sum will be brought down this year to provide us with a suitable building for both post office and customs purposes.

I support the hon. member
for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) in what he has said. Would not the government consider it a fair suggestion to give the city of Saskatoon better accommodation than it has at present? Regina has a very fine public building, while the city of Saskatoon, nearly of the same size, is without even a public building that can be called such. What we have there is nothing more than a makeshift, and the government is paying between $23,000 and $24,000 in rentals for space. As the hon. member says, the present site, which was purchased for a new post office, is not suitable. The building should be erected where the post office business is now carried on. Some years ago a contract was let for a building, but somehow or other it was suddenly cancelled. I do not know what the reason was. At any rate, one would think it only fair at least to spend impartially the available money. Regina is very well supplied while Saskatoon, as I say, has not even a public building worthy the name.

I do not object to
Saskatoon's claims, which I know are strong. What my hon. friend from that city has said is true. But the proposal now before the House comes, and has come for years, from the post office authorities to meet the demands of mechanical operation. It is true that the present post office is a fine looking building, but from the point of view of the immediate necessity for an extension it is not adequate. The revenue last year at Regina was $802,000, while that of Saskatoon was $285,000, not half as .much. I can well appreciate the argument that if Saskatoon had a post office large enough and sufficiently well equipped mechanically to handle the many functions of the postal service which now must be distributed because of lack of facilities, the revenue in thait city might be high. I merely make this statement to meet the view expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. Evans), that we should put first things first.

I repeat, I am not objecting to this vote; I support it. I say, however, that Saskatoon occupies a unique position. A great deal of its work is due to the transfer of mail, and better [Mr. A. M. Youns.l
accommodation is undoubtedly required. I am not asking for a public building immediately, but I hope that something will be done in the supplementary estimates. The building has been there a great many years. It was built for a city of ten thousand people, and it is now serving approximately thirty-five thousand. I would urge on the government again the advisability of getting all the facts and bringing down an estimate as early as possible.
Does the Minister of Railways say that property in Regina is valued at $3,000 a foot, or will a portion of this vote be used for the expropriation proceedings?

When the offer was made a year or more ago to purchase this property, the owners asked a price, including of course the building on the property, in pxcess I believe of $3,000 a front foot. The department did not believe the value was in it, and decided therefore to proceed by way of expropriation in order that the Exchequer court should decide what was the proper value of a piece of property of this kind taken under the circumstances that prevailed. The sum in the estimates is not by any means to decide the matter, but in order to give authority to the minister to proceed to expropriate and pay whatever sum the Exchequer court may decide to be the value of the property.

I think it is rather unfortunate that the minister has put in the estimates $150,000 for this additional site and then says he is going to expropriate, because those who own the property will undoubtedly produce the government's own estimate of its requirements as evidence in support of their claim as to the price. The procedure is simple. The Exchequer court sits on the case, and the owners of the property produce witnesses to bolster up their case. They will claim a certain price, probably beyond this, and among the evidence they produce will undoubtedly be this official estimate of the government of $150,000. This is not final, as the minister says, by any means. It does not decide the case, but it is supporting evidence and it strikes me that $3,000 a front foot is an abnormally high price for property in the city of Regina. I am not disputing what the minister said a minute ago about the importance of the city of Regina and the business they do there. It is an important centre and a very handsome revenue is collected there. All of that is admitted, but it is the method of approaching this question that I am speaking of, and I would say that

Supply-Public Works-Saskatchewan
you lose- your case before you go to the Exchequer court. Might I ask the minister whether in considering these expropriation proceedings the government have arrived at a figure which, they will first offer to the property holders, and on the other hand, have the government received from the owners of this property an offer of a price at which they will sell, between which two prices the decision has to be made.

The department have been notified by the owners of this cafe that they would not sell their property at S3,000 a foot frontage, as they claimed the property had enhanced in value, owing to the Canadian Pacific having decided to locate their hotel just two blocks south, on Scarth street. I say frankly that our reason for expropriating is that we could not get the property at what we considered a proper price. I do not admit that it is worth even $3,000 a foot, but they would not take that price.

Has the minister made
an offer?

I am informed there was
an offer of $3,000 a foot front, and that they refused it.

The committee is faced
now with the exact facts. An offer has been made of $3,000 a foot front, which the owners have refused, and the case is going to- the Exchequer court. We can therefore very properly say that the price will be something in excess of $3,000 a front foot, or $150,000. I do not wish to draw any invidious comparisons, but take for instance the case referred to a moment ago at Saskatoon. I am quite certain that it would not cost anything like that amount, comparatively speaking, to purchase a site in Saskatoon; it probably would not cost $1,000 a front foot, but here in the city of Regina-the capital city, it is true- you are paying $3,000 a front foot. To my mind it is an excessively high price.

One of the banks paid
more than that.

One of the curses of fixing the value of city property is the price the banks pay for selected corners. It is something scandalous. A bank will come into a town or city and pay an exorbitant price for some choice corner, but I do not consider that as an argument to support the government's action. I am not sufficiently acquainted with Regina to say whether it might not be better for Regina to consider another site altogether.

From the point of view
of the member for the city, I would much
prefer an entirely new public building, but unfortunately I am faced with the post office difficulty, and I must admit that the post office officials are right in their contention that they must have an addition more especially to the ground floor space of this building.
I should say that the owners of the building are not political friends of mine-
I am not suggesting that. That would not make a bit of difference to me.
They are good Tories.

The minister admits that
there are good Tories.

Sure, my hon. friend is
a good Tory. I should also say that one of the reasons for the price being high is, of course, that the owners of the building will claim damage with respect to the business.
I understand that.

There will be business
damages. I was informed that this vote was necessary in order to enable expropriation proceedings to commence, that before getting the authority of parliament it was very doubtful if any expropriation proceedings could be gone on with. I was not aware that an offer of any specific figure had been made by the Public Works department for the property, but I do know that the parties concerned refused to sell to anybody at S3,000 per front foot.

What is the value of
the present post office?
I have not those figures. It was built in 1912.
Could it be sold for anything like its present value?

Oh, no. It is a big building, but it is useful for no other purpose than that to which it is devoted. While the building is large, unfortunately it is not large on the ground floor, and the great problem of congestion is in connection with the postal facilities which must be handled on the ground floor.

Although it is
not usual for Moose Jaw to find a friend in Regina, I must say that the post office in Regina is on perhaps the most valuable piece of property in the whole city. During the last few years Regina in proportion to its population has grown perhaps more than any other city in Canada; it is going ahead very rapidly. The post office property is very valuable, and I do not doubt that the

Supply-Public Works-Alberta
restaurant is also very valuable from a business standpoint. I agree with the Minister of Railways that added floor space is needed in the city of Regina. I have known the city and its business for some time, and there is great congestion in the post office. There is not room in that building for a post office for a city the size of Regina, and1 I do not think there is anything out of the way in this vote.

Item agreed to.
Tisdale-public building, $12,000.
Could we have an explanation of that?

This is required to purchase a site and to pay for the erection of a public building for postal service at Tisdale. The proposed building will be a one-storey brick structure, 32 feet 6 inches by 29 feet 6 inches. The estimated cost will be $8,500 for the building, $1,800 for fittings, $800 for grading and sidewalk and $900 for contingencies, total $12,000.
Have you a site there?
No, we are asking for money to purchase the site.

The revenue at Tisdale is
nearly $3,000 less than at Biggar.

Item agreed to.
Alberta-Dominion	public	buildings-improvements, repairs, etc., $17,000.

This is generally for the
repair of all the public buildings owned by the department in Alberta.

I am not going to ask
the minister to build a post office in Calgary, although we need one; but I want to place certain facts before him in that regard. The post office was situated in the centre of the city on a site 100 feet by 120. My good friends to my right pulled it down and instead of building a post office they put up a fine armoury. They were going to build a post office. I am not censuring my friends to my right for not doing so, because the war broke out and the post office could not be built. At the same time all that is left there is an unsightly hole in the ground surrounded by a board fence about eight feet high. We have never had a post office since. It has migrated to three different places. First it went to Second street east, opposite the city hall; then it went to the Lancaster building on Eighth avenue west, and now it is in the Southam building on First street west. We do expect 
that before the lease expires the government will take into consideration the advisability of replacing the post office and I suggest that the government should do something at least to -beautify that spot, and take into consideration the advisability of replacing the building which was torn down. The fence is a hideous one and should be removed.

Is there any provision in
this estimate for neeeded repairs to the public building at'Lethbridge?

It will cover that. Public
buildings generally are covered by this vote.

At the'request of some of my friends I visited the building and I will tell the minister that the building is settling and it needs decorating and repairing very badly. The minister perhaps knows that this building houses the post office, the Dominion land office and the income tax office. I wish the minister would look into this matter.

I am much obliged for the information. I was not aware of the settling of the building to which the hon. member refers. If it is something which is within reasonable limits it will be covered by this amount, and if not we will have to provide other means.
The matter has been reported; it is within the knowledge of the government inspector at Calgary.

Will the minister tell me if there is any truth in the story that the government is considering purchasing the Southam building at the expiration of the lease instead of getting a new post office? I shall be glad to confer with the minister further in regard to this matter.
I have heard nothing of it. The lease does not expire for a couple of 3'ears.

Item agreed to.
Wainwright-public building, $15,000.

Could the minister give us a better explanation to-day than he gave us a few days ago why the vote for the public building at Camrose, placed in the supplementary estimates last year, has been left out?
I am afraid I cannot give any better explanation to-day.
A cabinet secret.
No.

The policy as to the construction of public buildings was determined,
I understand, on the question of urgency.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
I do not deny the necessity of the building at Wainwright, but will the minister tell us that there is a greater urgency for the building at Wainwright than for the building at Cam-rose?

From the information I have, there is urgency for the building at Wainwright, and there is a site available there. The matter has been under consideration for a number of years-since 1913, I think. It may be assumed that at that time a public building was considered necessary, and since then it has been pressed upon the government very frequently. The postal revenue of W'ainwright is $6,313, and the building that is proposed to be erected would cost only $10,500.
What is the population?
About a thousand.

Will the minister compare
those facts with the facts in relation to the Camrose building?
I shall be very glad to do so.
Will the minister give the committee the facts in regard to Camrose as to revenue and population, just as he has given them in the other case?
My hon. friend will readily understand that I have details only in regard to the items which appear in the estimates.
The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) can help my hon. friend out.

The town of Camrose has a population of over two thousand. The gross annual revenue from the post office is $16,561, and from the sub-customs office over $50,000. The government still hold a lot which I believe was purchased in 1912 or 1913. The request for a post office was placed before the government last year, when they considered it of sufficient urgency to include a vote for it in the supplementary estimates, but I regret to say that the item does not appear in these main estimates for some reason or other. I dhould be glad to have the minister explain why the item has been cut out. Otherwise the idea will prevail that urgency is not one of the factors considered by the government in providing for new public buildings.

I should like to ask the
minister a question along the same lines as
that which I asked him a few minutes ago. I notice that in 1926 there was spent in Saskatchewan $20,919, while in the present estimates the total expenditure is $205,450- ten times more.
Hear, hear.

Oh yes, that is fine, that
is the way the west is going all over. But contrast this with what the government is doing for Alberta. In 1926 the expenditure there amounted to $45,422, but in these estimates the total provided for is only $32,000-a decrease of 25 per cent.

What about British
Columbia?

I will deal with British
Columbia when we come to the votes for my province.

Surely the
member for the constituency in which Wainwright is situated will stand up for his own post office?	.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, March 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. 78, respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. A. McPHERSON (Portage la Prairie):
subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the debate closed the other evening the Clerk Assistant was helping me by reading a document, and I suppose the proper thing would be for him to continue. If for any reason he has mislaid that clipping or forgotten that he was my assistant on that occasion, with the permission of the House I will go on.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: He has lost the clipping.

subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I can assure hon.
gentlemen that it was a very fine clipping, well worth inserting in the records of this House. At that time I was discussing the question of how the province of Ontario was handling its own power, and a certain amount of objection was taken to my statement that this power was being disposed of to private

Georgian Bay Canal Company
interests. The clipping then being read was for the purpose of giving some idea of the conditions which were said to exist in northern Ontario. If I am wrong in my contention it is all the more reason why the matter should be investigated by a committee, as I suggested, in order that the facts may be properly ascertained regardless of our personal opinions. I have here another clipping which is so printed that I can read it, and it is rather interesting in view of the argument which is going on. This clipping is taken from the Ottawa Journal of March 11, and is headed:
Ask For Information Upper Ottawa Power Power Concession at Des Joachims May Be Sought
That the running streams commission of the province of Quebec is anticipating a request for a report from the Quebec legislature on the power resources of the Ottawa river, with a view to dealing with a request for development, is the information given from an authoritative source close to the Quebec government.
The announcement is in keeping with the trend of events along the river, particularly at Des Joachims, where gangs of men believed to be in the employ of the International Pulp and Paper, or allied interests, were busy all last summer, and where preparations are being made for another season's work.
The informer volunteered the information that the running streams commission is hastening its task of securing all possible data as to power development at Des Joachims. He states that the Ontario government too, in addition to that of Quebec, is to be approached with the view to securing a power concession at this point and that just as soon as the question of the renewal of the Georgian bay canal charter is settled, action will be speedy.	'
That is just another indication of the fact that while public ownership and the protection of the public are largely discussed there are other people who are interested in this power development scheme on the Ottawa river.
The original act in connection with this project, I submit, is of very great importance in this discussion, and I note with considerable satisfaction that in one particular I agree with some of the previous speakers. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) in speaking the other night stated that the original charter in connection with this work was primarily for the purpose of building a canal, and later in the debate that opinion was supported by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart). I agree with the hon. gentleman in that statement; the original charter as drafted would indicate that the main purpose of the charter was the construction of a canal. The hon. member for Grenville-Dun-das (Mr. Casselman) remarked in the course

of his address that the original charter did not authorize the production of electric power, but I would like to take a few moments to read the clause of the original charter of 1894 which has to do with that matter. The first clauses have to do with the construction of a canal, but there was a further clause inserted as follows:
Lay out and lease or otherwise dispose of water lots and use, sell, lease or otherwise dispose of water brought by or for the said canals or works but not requisite for-the same, and produce, lease and supply, or otherwise dispose of hydraulic, electric and other kinds of power in connection with the works hereby authorized.
That was the original clause (g), which received a rather substantial amendment in chapter 123 of the statutes of 1912, when the whole clause was repealed and the following
substituted therefor:
Produce, lease and supply, or otherwise dispose of surplus hydraulic, electric and other kinds of power developed in connection with and for the purposes of the works hereby authorized, the rates or prices at or for which such hydraulic and electric power may be disposed of by the company to be fixed or determined by the Board of Baihvay Commissioners for Canada in accordance with the provisions of section 360a of the Railway Act.
My first comment on that clause, both as it was originally and as amended, is that I think there is no doubt that power is given the company to produce and sell electric energy. But I want to draw the attention of hon. gentlemen to this very important section which appears both in the original clause and in the amendment. That is, the company is allowed to produce these various kinds of power which are developed in connection with and for the purposes of the works authorized by this charter. I submit to the House that the only interpretation which can fairly be put upon that clause is that any power produced must be in connection with the canal. This matter is so serious that I would not ask this House to take my opinion as to the exact legal interpretation of this clause, but I suggest that if the charter is primarily for the purpose of building a canal, it is a fair interpretation for a reasonable man to say that in building power plants they must do so in connection with the works authorized by the charter. I submit that that would indicate that if they did not proceed with the work authorized their power under the charter would be exceeded. That may be open to debate, may be open to legal argument, and if so the courts are there to settle the interpretation. The company would have to go to the courts

Georgian Bay Canal Company
if there was any dispute on that interpretation and see w7hat the exact conditions were-they would take that chance.
Now as to the canal itself: While a great deal of interest is taken by others in the power project, personally I have no interest in it. I am, however, interested in this canal, and the consensus of opinion of this House seems to be that a canal from Montreal to the Georgian bay would be a very valuable thing to the Dominion. It also seems to be undisputed that it is a feasible undertaking. I submit that the west is interested in having this canal. It should assist in settling the transportation problem. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) in his remarks the other night pointed out that the charter was first granted a long time ago and that conditions have since changed. I think he mentioned the construction of the Transcontinental railway, the Welland canal and the Panama canal as reasons why this project was not so necessary. I agree that the construction of that railway and the canals referred to does affect this canal project and might not make it so desirable; but it is a good maxim in any line of business administration to scrap old machinery if you can get cheaper and better results by introducing improvements. I do not think that will be necessary in this case, but the idea that you are precluded from getting better results because of existing conditions is not debatable. I was rather surprised that although the hon. member for Leeds went on and showed that this enterprise was not necessary and should not be allowed, at the conclusion of his remarks he expressed the opinion that the proper thing to do was for the government to build it. Now if the canal should not be built by private individuals because it is not necessary, I submit it is not advisable for the government to construct it at a loss to the country. Furthermore, I think that the government is not in a position at the present time to expend the large sums of money that would be necessary to build this canal, regardless altogether of the power development scheme. It would be an enormous undertaking, and this Dominion has heavy enough liabilities at the present time. I do not know how long it would take this country to get into a position to carry out the project and be able to afford the money. The estimated cost, as I understand it, of the canal and power project would be somewhere between two hundred and fifty and three hundred and fifty millions. A large proportion of this would be expended for dams,
without taking into consideration the expenditure involved in the construction of the power plants. Therefore I quite agree that the Dominion government could not undertake this project at the present time. It might be fifty years, it might be a hundred years- I am not certain what the exact period would be-but it would be a good many years before we could undertake such a huge expenditure.

Mj\ McPHERSON: I have already argued, although my hon. friend does not seem to understand the argument, that under this charter they have to build this canal before they can use the power, and that is the reason why I want this bill to go to committee. The value of this canal I think is not in dispute. Reflect for a moment upon what it means by the opening up of northern Ontario, the opening up of the waterways from Port Arthur to the ocean, and the value it -would be to Canada as a whole, and it is evident we shall have to be very careful before we say we will not even consider this matter in committee.
In closing, because it is not my intention to delay this matter by a long speech-I have tried to keep to the essential facts as closely as I could-let me say that I am in favour of this bill going to the committee in the first place because I do not think the reason

But I should like to put this question to hon. gentlemen who may have been in this House in 1912: at whose request and under whose direction was the amendment of 1912 inserted in the act? I am informed that it was at the request of the late Sir Adam Beck on behalf of the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario. I do not know for certain but I am told that he was present and drafted that clause to protect the interests of that hydro-electric commission. Whether or not that is so can be ascertained. I understand that only in two cases in the last twenty-five years has there been a refusal to send bills to the committee. If my explanation of why the provision in subclause (g) was introduced in 1912 is not correct, then I say this: that before this charter is renewed there should1 be provisions inserted in the bill which will prohibit the applicants or the charter holders from making any profit out of power developments until the canal is complete.
