speechtext:
Unlike my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. McPherson) I am opposed to this bill going to the select standing committee of this House for consideration. It may be true as my hon. friend has stated that only in a few instances have private bills in this House been defeated upon the motion for second reading. But it is equally true that seldom have private bills been introduced involving questions of so great magnitude and of such great consequence to the people of Canada in general as the bill which is under discussion now and which stands upon the motion for second reading. I realize that upon the second reading of a bill we discuss the principles of the bill rather than its details. I am unalterably opposed to the prin-

ciple of this bill and I desire to record my opposition to it when the time for so doing shall arrive. In opposing this bill upon its second reading, I feel sure that I am on firm ground and that I am following established parliamentary practice both in this country and in Great Britain when a private bill of this nature is proposed in parliament. My authority for my position is pretty well summed up in the thirteenth edition of May's parliaments^' procedure at page 709, where it is said:
The second reading of a private bill, corresponds with the same stage in other bills, and in agreeing to it the House affirms the general principle, or expediency, of the measure. There is, however, a distinction between the second reading of a public and of a private bill, which should not be overlooked. A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the House, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons: but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the House, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee. Where,. irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the House will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee. This is the first occasion on which a bill is brought before the House otherwise than pro forma,-
That is to say, the second reading.
-or in connection with the standing orders; and if the bill be opposed, upon its principle, it is the proper time for attempting its defeat.
I oppose this bill on principle. I consider it thoroughly bad in principle and if passed it will prove worse in practice; and I intend to record my vote, when the time comes, as opposed to it. Before concluding my remarks, I shall place in your hands, Mr. Speaker, an amendment in the fol'lownig words:
That all the words after the word "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
The character and object of this bill involve matters of grave national and provincial importance, and are such as to constitute it a measure of public policy which ought not to be dealt with by any private bill.
This amendment h.as been framed in accordance with recognized precedent in this House in such cases. The bill before us, Mr. Speaker, involves, I submit, very grave questions of public policy. I doubt whether that statement will be denied in any section of the House. I cannot conjure up before my mind any graver matter of public policy ait this moment in Canada than the great ques-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
tion of transportation. We have in this bill a proposal thait a private corporation shall construct a great transportation work, in this country over a course of waterway estimated at about 200 miles, and when that work is constructed it will be a means of carrying tlhe great products of the Canadian west to the Canadian east or to Europe and the products of the east back to the Canadian we^t-a project which one only needs to state to convince oneself of its importance and of its thoroughly national aspect.
But there is another view of the matter which the House will readily appreciate. This transportation work, if ever constructed, will be at once a competitor with other transportation lines which 'this country owns and operates and which we all regard as great national undertakings. During recent years we have spent well on to $100,000,000 on the Welland canal for the purpose of improving a waterway from the west to the east and on to Europe. We are proceeding with that expenditure to-day but the Welland canal is not our final goal: once we are through the Welland canal we must go on to the St. Lawrence and have a completed waterway. The object of the present bill is to construct another great canal by private interests to compete directly with the millions which we have already invested in our present waterway a few miles south of the one proposed. We have in this country, moreover, another transportation system, upon which we have expended hundreds upon hundreds of millions of dollars of Canadian money, known as the Canadian National Railways, a great national undertaking in the success of which every comer of the Dominion is interested. This bill proposes to incorporate a private undertaking to construct a work to be carried on in opposition to and in competition with the two established transportation systems in Canada owned by the Canadian people. When one considers these facts, can one hestitate for a moment to decide that this bill deals directly with a matter of public policy and not of private interest in any sense of the word?
There are many other considerations of a distinctly public nature involved in this proposal. The rights of the Dominion and the rights of two great provinces are directly concerned, and these must be taken into account. I agree that until recent years provincial rights as 'opposed to Dominion rights have not perhaps been very well settled. But through a long succession of decisions in our courts of justice and in the privy council these rights have now been so 32649-72
well determined and adjusted 'that we all know and recognize them when they are stated. Involved in this proposed work is an interprovincial river dividing the great province of Quebec from the province of Ontario, and we know that on either side of that river, all the land is under the jurisdiction of the legislatures of one or other of these provinces. We know that the provinces own the land; we know that the provinces own the beds of the river right to the middle; we know that the provinces own and control the water in the river; we know that the provinces own and control even the fish in these waters. All, therefore, that this parliament is concerned with is its paramount right in respect of the single question of navigation; that is the only authority which the parliament of Canada can exercise over an interprovincial river. This bill seeks to interfere with provincial rights; it proposes to' grant, as an incidental power, the right to utilize for electrical development the water of the Ottawa river and to a certain extent -the land on either side of the river, irrespective of the authority of the provinces of Quebec and of Ontario. Surely that is a matter of public policy; surely it is a matter which involves a great principle. And it is a matter of too great magnitude and too great consequence to be entrusted to any private individuals or to any private corporation. Why, one has only to state the case to realize its gravity and importance. On the Ottawa river it is said that over 1,000,000 horse-power of electrical energy can be developed. This potential power is the property of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; it is so to-day. On the French river, which is entirely, I think, within the province of Ontario, it is said that there is another large amount of electrical power available. Ontario to-day is suffering from a lack of electrical power, and Ontario is looking to the Ottawa river to supply a very necessary demand. The province of Quebec to-day is suffering from a shortage of electrical power, and is stretching out in every direction in its own province to supply the demand. Should we permit a private company, should we permit any body of individuals to come to this parliament and say:	We ask you
to confer upon us rights which will supersede all provincial claims; we ask you to recognize and restore a charter granted to us 'by this parliament thirty-three years ago, and to give us further time to construct a work to compete directly with two great national undertakings of this country; we ask you to give us a renewal of authority to construct a work which may deprive both Ontario and

Georgian Bay Canal Company

Quebec of a wealth of electrical power which the provinces to-day rightly own.
Is this not a matter of grave public concern? Is this not a matter of grave public policy? Is this not a matter which involves a great principfe? We in this House must decide upon this question of principles. The highest parliamentary authority in Great Britain or in this country from whom I have quoted supports my contention. May's Parliamentary Procedure is the standard, and May distinctly asserts that the appropriate stage at which to object to the principle of a private bill is upon the motion for second reading. The amendment which I have proposed will afford every member of this House an opportunity of deciding upon that principle. Such was the object which I had in moving the amendment, my main object, of course, being to destroy this measure, to blot it out.
I do not attach very much weight to the argument of hon. members who say: Oh, let it go to the committee. If we do, we will have approved the principle of the bill, and as I said before, I am unalterably opposed to the principle of this bill.
I am not going to prolong my remarks upon this occasion, at all events, Mr. Speaker. I am going to place in your hands now the amendment which I have just read, and which I shall read again. It is moved by myself, and seconded by the hon. member for Argen-teuil (Sir George Perley):
That all the words after the word "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
The character and object of this bill involve matters of grave national and provincial importance, and are such as to constitute it a measure of public policy which ought not to be dealt with by any private bill.
Mr. T L.. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) : Mr. Speaker, I am opposed both to the motion and the amendment before the House. It is on the second reading of a bill that its principle must be considered. The province of Ontario will soon find out where the two political parties in this honourable House stand so far as the development of water-power is concerned.
I want to say to my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. McPherson) that there is no province suffering to-day from corporation rule worse than the province of Manitoba. From the Nipigon river westward, all the water-powers of this country have been given over to American millionaires.
This particular bill, Mr. Speaker, first came before this House in 1894. It has survived thirty-three years. It first came up before the diamond jubilee of our late beloved Queen

Victoria. It ran through the reign of King Edward VII, and survived through to the reign of King George V. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it makes this parliament look ridiculous in the eyes of the free citizens of this country to-day that after thirty-three years we should again have this bill before us. Sir Clifford Sifton, -who is our arch enemy in the matter of water-powers, wants to grab the whole water-powers of. the Ottawa valley. Sir Clifford Sifton has been dominating the west for many years. It is he who is responsible for all the railway ills of this country through tying up the Canadian Pacific to the Crows-nest pass agreement, which is the basis of the rate structure of this country, past, present and future, and if the west is suffering to-day from lack of development of its water-powers and from corporation rule, it is due to the fact that Sir Clifford Sifton in the past has been able to dominate in the Liberal party.
The Liberal party is on trial to-night in this House before the citizens of this country. What is the policy of the government to-day on this particular bill, this bill which has survived under nine prime ministers, under two kings and three queens of this great empire, under eight or nine parliaments, and is again today before this House after thirty-three years during which not a spadeful of earth has been dug on this canal? We have seen the Liberals of Saskatchewan and Manitoba rising in this House to-night and shedding buckets of tears over this multi-millionaire Sir Clifford Sifton, who wants now to grab all the water-powers of the Ottawa valley.
This is not the first time that I have opposed this bill. I was down opposing it with our late beloved leader of the hydro project in Ontario. Sir Adam Beck may be dead today, but his principles will live forever throughout Ontario. I well remember coming down with him and appearing before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and hydro had very few friends then in either the Conservative or the Liberal party. I well remember the time when Sir Adam Beck and I were howled down in the railway committee by a large number of gentlemen in the session of 1912. We were here again in 1913, again in 1915, and again in 1918, and I think the last time we were down here to oppose this particular bill was when I was chief magistrate for the city of Toronto in 1921.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie argued again to-night, as he did last Tuesday, that the company will have to build the canal features first. The canal features of this bill, Mr. Speaker, are a huge joke, and the joker is in the bill. It is ten times

Georgian Bay Canal Company
worse than the Newmarket canal. Did anybody ever hear of the Liberal party doing anything with regard to that canal except making a political football of it? The people of North York got tired of them, and they defeated the Prime Minister, the leader of the Liberal party, in 1925. Where does the Liberal party stand to-night on this particular bill? It would make a political football of the Ottawa river to-day, just as it tried to do of the Niagara river. In the railway committee last session, I asked what was the policy of the government regarding the Red lake bill? I had the opportunity of talking that bill out, on five or six different nights, and I am prepared to talk this bill out, if necessary, on ten or fifteen nights, because my constituents expect me to do it. I want to know where the Prime 'Minister stands in regard to this bill. Let me quote from the Toronto Globe, a good Liberal paper, the paper of George Brown.
I look to you, Mr. Speaker, as one of the shining lights of Liberalism in this country to-day. You have never deserted your principles. You stood like a bulwark when others of the Liberal party were willing to surrender the west. You and your predecessor, two of the most brilliant postmasters general, fought that bill to the death. But the Liberal party were captured by the Globe and the Globe pressed for concession after concession with the result that Sir Clifford Sifton is to blame for all the present railway ills of this country. Millions and millions of dollars have been wasted because of mistakes made by Sir Clifford Sifton. You, Mr. Speaker, and Sir William Mulock fought hard to save the Liberal party from being corporationized at that particular time. Sir Clifford Sifton has never built anything in this country. He has made a football out of this particular bill. The Sifton interests are the same as the Holt interests; they are trying to fight each other behind a smoke screen. They are part and parcel of a group of American multimillionaires trying to get this country by the throat. I am surprised at those of the Progressive party who come from Ontario not rising to the defence of the principles for which Sir Adam Beck fought and died. Sir Adam had to fight corporations all his life, but he lived to see his principles respected by Ontario and by Canada.
To-day I ask the government where they stand in this country. Are they prepared to announce their policy regarding the fourteenth renewal of this charter, one of the most iniquitous charters which ever came before this House? The Conservative party stands 32649-72J
on trial; so does the Liberal party, and the party system stands or falls by what we do with this particular bill. The people of this country will not any longer stand for the handing over of our water-powers and the wealth of this Dominion to a number of Americans who have come over to Canada and who have found it a happy hunting ground for many years past. Let me say to those who come from Ontario that Sir Adam Beck's work will live for generations. He was the greatest protectionist leader this country ever produced. As Mr. Bruce, the Prime Minister of Australia, said a month or two ago, the work of Sir Adam Beck stands as one of the most marvelous achievements of the age, something of which Canada and the British Empire might well be proud. Ontario should revere that great statesman's memory long enough to defeat this bill.
My respected leader, the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has always been a good hydro man. In fact he is a city solicitor and one of the counsel for the hydro in his municipality. I believe the motion before the chair, while it does not go as far as I would like, will have the same effect- that of killing the bill. The Liberal party stands on trial in regard to this particular issue. There are only a few Liberals left in Ontario, and after the Liberal party line up, as I expect them to do in a few days, there will be very few of them left in Ontario. I doubt if there will be many of them left in Manitoba, 'Saskatchewan and Allberta, because the people are wakening up to the magnificent resources which they have in those particular provinces.
In to-day's Globe there is an editorial sounding the call to arms of the Liberals of this country. The Globe has not deserted the Liberal party; it is the Liberal party that has deserted the Globe and the principles of George Brown. The Globe to-day stands before the people of Ontario in a position in which it has never stood before. It is taking a front place to-day in supporting the platform and policy of Sir Adam Beck in that province. The Globe comes out to-day with an editorial asking where the Liberal party stands. The Liberal party must either stand or fall by their policy in this House. I do not see the much honoured and respected young Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the chamber to-night. I see the beloved Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe)- because he is beloved by his own party and

Georgian Bay Canal Company
by many on this side of the House. The Globe editorial reads:
Let the Government Speak
For four days now the Dominion parliament has discussed the Georgian Bay Canal Bill in the hours devoted to private members' bills. On each occasion the bill has been talked out. Has the time not come when the government should declare itself on the measure? The Globe believes it has, and is convinced that the great importance of the issue demands an expression of governmental opinion. In saying this the Globe does not forget that the government is not responsible for bills of private members, and may be quite within its rights in refusing to commit itself for or against a private measure. But the importance of the issue in the present instance more than warrants a departure from precedent.
Whether this 33-year old charter is renewed or not is a matter of first importance to two great provinces of the Dominion. With a unanimous voice the legislature of Ontario has spoken strongly against the renewal of the charter and protested to the Dominion government against what it considers to be an unwarranted usurpation of the water-power rights of the province. Surely in response to such a protest the government ought to declare itself. Mr. A. Clair Casselman, Conservative member for Grenville, on Tuesday urged the ministry, in fairness to itself, to state to the people where it stood with reference to what it termed the "power grab".
It is not a "power grab" at all. Newspapers on both sides in this province have been calling the Chicago diversion of water a "water steal," but the Chicago diversion of water is only a miniature steal. This grab of power in the Ottawa valley is a steal on the part of the Siftons.
"The government is laying itself open to rather serious charges," he said, and further added: "I would suggest that, since we are now on our fourth day on this matter in the House, the government should suggest to us what it is its intention to do; whether it is going to support the charter or whether it is not.
It has happened in the past, and may happen in the present instance, that government members have voted against one another on a private bill. But neither this nor any other consideration of precedent or custom should prevent an expression of governmental opinion on this important matter. The government should declare where it stands on the measure, and do it now.
Where is the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Euler) to-night? In the days when Sir Adam Beck was alive he boasted that he was a hydro man. The hon. member for North Bruce, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, (Mr. Malcolm) did the same thing. They were ready to stand up on political platforms in Bruce and Waterloo counties and say: we are hydro supporters; we will defend the principles for which Sir

Adam Beck fought and died. If we look at the Ottawa valley, we see that the whole of eastern Ontario has been stagnant for the past twenty-five years. Why? Because the Liberal party in eastern Ontario did not believe in Sir Adam Beck; they believed in private ownership, with the result to-day that the Ottawa valley right up to Nipissing and the Mattawa river is under the control of whom? Of American multi-millionaires, and more territory west of the Quebec boundary right up to the Nipigon river has been ceded to Americans than was ceded in the days of George III.
The hon. member for Portage lla Prairie (Mr. McPherson) the other evening in this House read an article from a Cochrane paper about the Abitibi Electric Development Company, and he blamed the hydro for it. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that he did not know what he was talking about. The Abitibi Electric Development Company was a privately-owned concern. In 1905, 1906, 1907 and 1908 I was one of a deputation of hydro men who went to aSk the Ontario government to electrify the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario in order to aid in the development of the Ottawa valley right up to Cochrane and to carry the boon of cheap light and power from the water-powers of the great province of Ontario to the mining camps in the northern part of the Ottawa valley. The failure to act in this matter was one of the very few mistakes made by Sir James Whitney. The Conservative party of Ontario deserve all) the credit for the hydro-electric movement. Talk of that movement being in polities! It must stay in politics until we get all the water-powers not only of the Ottawa valley but of new Ontario. Let me tell the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. McPherson) that the corporations were so influential that they kept Sir Adam Beck out of new Ontario, with the result that to-day the Abitibi Company, according to the article read the other night in this House, are going to charge the town of Cochrane and the mining companies in the neighbourhood at the rate of S75 per horsepower. Who is to blame for that? The people of new Ontario, because they allowed themselves to be deluded by the subsidized press of that section of the country which shouted from the housetops in favour of the corporation.
This bill is one of the most monstrous outrages that was ever perpetrated on this country. It is not a canal proposition at all. A lot of Liberal members from Manitoba are only too willing to take it for granted that the proposed canal will be constructed, but

Public Works-Alberta
I can tell those hon. gentlemen that instead of a spade being used to turn the first sod for a canal it will be put in the ground to bury them, not only politically but otherwise. This canal has the Newmarket canal beaten forty ways. I wish Gilbert and Sullivan were alive to write a comic opera on this wonderful canal about which the hon. member for Portage la Prairie seems to be somewhat concerned. Again I assure him that he need feel no uneasiness whatever-the canal will never be built. The proposition has been referred to in many elections in the Ottawa valley and has no doubt proved very useful in providing campaign funds for many candidates in that territory, just as the Newmarket canal served a similar purpose in North York.
Last session, Mr. Speaker, I urged that we should go through the statute books and find out how many of these paper companies are still holding charters that may affect power developments for the benefit of the people. This charter stands in the way of Ontario utilizing the water-powers of the Ottawa river. But as for the canal, it is all paper; there is no water in it at all. The first charter was secured away back in the days of good old Queen Victoria, in 1894, two years before Sir Wilfrid Laurier made Canada a nation. The promoters came to the House again in 1898 and secured a renewal, the incorporators numbering ninety-seven and being composed of all the politicians, great and small, in the city of Ottawa. It -will be noted that the incorporators were only three less than the celebrated committee of a hundred. It was proposed by chapter 108 of the statutes of 1898 that the company should have sixteen provisional directors. The promoters came back to parliament in 1900 for a further extension of time, and found it hard work to get six gentlemen to act as provisional directors. During the general election of 1900 we heard a great deal about this canal in the Ottawa valley and about the Newmarket canal in the Toronto district. My young friend from Parkdale, as a member of the Parkdale Canoe Club, was supposed to take his canoe up the shining waters of the Newmarket canal and then through the Trent system to Georgian bay and thence by this long-promised canal down the Ottawa river.
Another application for a further extension of time was made in 1904, and the promoters then undertook to go full steam ahead with the canal. They had been to England and interested a good old Britisher by the name of Sir Robert Perks, who came out here and went over the proposed route of the canal.
On the strength of this it was said that contracts had been let for the work, but strange to say, not a sod was turned. The only canal we have in the Ottawa valley so far is the canal in front of the Chateau Laurier, and along the banks of that canal we see a few rowboats, which I suppose represent Canada's navy.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at six o'clock we were considering item 140-$16,000 for a public building at Wain-wright, Alberta.

The minister has told U3
that urgency is the factor which determines whether or not public buildings shall be erected. In looking over the list I find that to Kensington with a revenue of about $3,000 we voted $12,000; to Baie St. Paul, with a revenue of about $3,600 we voted $20,000; to Kenogami, with a revenue of about $7,000 we voted $27,000 and to Limoilou, with a revenue of about $5,000 we voted $50,000. Then in Ontario to Durham, with a revenue of about $6,300 we voted $20,000; to Rockland, with a revenue of about $2,800, we voted $25,000, and to Tisdale, Saskatchewan, with a revenue of about $7,000 we voted $12,000. In the item now before us, however, we find' Wainwright, with a revenue of $6,313, being voted $15,000. If these amounts have been voted to these various places on account of urgency, I would point out that Camrose has a revenue of $16,500 and is therefore entitled to the very best consideration by the government. In addition to that, the customs office there produces a revenue of over $50,000 annually. Camrose is one of the most flourishing towns in Alberta, and the postal authorities have agreed that if any public buildings for postal purposes were to be constructed in Alberta Camrose should receive first consideration. It is a very important railway centre, with lines radiating from it in eight different directions; it has a very fine normal school which accommodates several hundred students every year, and I know the present post office is taxed beyond its capacity. I feel sure that this has been an oversight on th,e part of the government; I would not want to think this item was dropped for any other reason, and I am going to ask the minister if he will not

Supply-Public Works-Alberta
give this very favourable consideration, and place in the supplementary estimates an amount sufficient to take care of the construction of a public building in that town.

I cannot give my hon.
friend any further reply than I have already given. I might repeat what I have already said to him, but I do not know that that would assist matters. This matter will be considered with the various other applications for public buildings, of which there are many, and they will all receive the best consideration we can possibly give.
Would not the minister go so far as to say that he would give this particular matter his favourable consideration?
I cannot say that.

Perhaps the minister
will tell us why it was given favourable consideration in the estimates last year?

I was not in charge of
the department at that time.

Do I understand that
the change of ministers has brought about a change in the policy of the department? It would appear that that has been so, when places like Tisdale and Kensington can get new post offices.
I do not like to hear a good Prince Edward Islander continually taking up the question of the Kensington post office; I must take exception to that.

I do not know just
what my hon. friend means by a "good" Prince Edward Islander. I know the village of Kensington very well; it is a delightful and splendid little place, but there are hundreds of places in western Canada just as nice and larger which have never dreamed of getting a post office. I made a reference to one such town near my own home, and there are many even larger places, more deserving of post offices, which cannot get them. There are many incorporated towns of considerable size in which I would like to see public buildings, but I realize that we cannot get them all. I do think, however, that when the money is being spent it should be distributed as nearly as possible according to the needs, and the needs should be based as much as possible on the revenue of the post pffices. I am criticizing this item because of the amount of money being spent in comparison to the revenue derived.

I would like to support
the contention of the hon. member for Cam-rose (Mr. Lucas) that there should be a post office built in that town, because after all is said and done Camrose is bringing in a large revenue to the government. I cannot understand why this item was dropped from the estimates. So far as the item under discussion goes, I know the locality very well indeed, and recognize that the reason a new building was requested, is that the present premises are very inadequate. The town of Wainwright is of some importance as a tourist centre, and as we all know, the largest buffalo park in the world is located near it. It is also the centre of a coming oil field, and there is every reason why a new building worthy of the town should be constructed.

There is just one point to which I would like to draw the attention of the minister, more particularly when he is making up the supplementary estimates. If you go through the items you will find that practically every province has had an increase in the expenditures to be made, with the one exception of Alberta, for which province the expenditure has been reduced. When the supplementary estimates are being made up I would suggest that this fact be taken into account.

For the life of me I cannot understand why, when an amount was included for the Camrose post office in the supplementary estimates for last year, it should be dropped from the estimates this year. It does seem to me that in consideration of the revenue from the post office and customs office, and with the population and business done in that place, the minister would be well advised to maintain this item in the estimates for this year. Only $32,000 is being spent in the whole province of Alberta this year; $17,000 is for general repairs to public buildings, something required every year, and the remainder is made up of this single item of $15,000 for the post office at Wain wright. I have a feeling that this matter is not being dealt with in absolute fairness, and I am going to urge the minister, as the hon. member for Camrose has done, to reconsider this matter and include this item in the supplementary estimates.

May I, as a member from Ontario, support the hon. member for Cam-rose in the attitude he has taken, and I would like to point out to the minister that we might be a little more frank in these discussions. We have heard a number of members get up and say they do not understand why this item

Supply-Public Works-British Columbia
was cut out. We all frankly admit why it was cut out-it was because the member for Camrose dlid not vote with the government last year. There is no use beating about the bush. The same thing happened in the constituency of Queen's-Lunenburg: the item in that case was cut out of the supplementary estimates after the election of the present member. If the minister can confound my reasoning by reinserting these items in the supplementaries I shall be glad to see him do it.

Item agreed to.
British Columbia-public works, $243,262.
Bentinck island lazaretto-new buildings, $5,000.

In connection with the
British Columbia vote I should like just to draw attention to the policy advanced by the Minister of Public Works in which he indicated that public buildings would be provided where there was not adequate provision already and where urgent necessity for better accommodation existed. Now this meagre vote for public buildings in British Columbia suggests that the Minister of Health, who is the direct representative of the province in the cabinet, must be exercising his political prejudices against British Columbia because it gave the Conservatives a popular majority of nearly
100,000.	There is no other construction to be placed on the fact that we are not getting very much in the way of public buildings in British Columbia. We know that under the generalship of the Minister of Health, who had charge of the British Columbia campaign, the only Liberal returned from that province was the minister himself; and curiously enough in the whole eastern half of the province the only vote for a public building is in the district represented by the minister himself.
Now I want to follow entirely the line of policy indicated by the minister. In the district of East Kootenay, represented by the Minister of Health, there is one vote for $5,500 for a public building in the town of Kimberley. Kimberley will be very glad to hear that news; yet at the same time I submit it will be disappointed, because it is one of the thriving communities of British Columbia, and should have a vote of $25,000. It has a population of three or four thousand, and certainly a $5,000 vote is inadequate for a place which has practically the richest silver-lead mine on the whole American continent. There are many local improvements going on there, and among the communities in the province that should be able to lay claim to a
public building Kimberley certainly is one. The fact of the matter is that the Minister of Health owes a great deal to the community of Kimberley. I do not blame the Minister of Public Works for all the contentious discussion that has been going on in this House this afternoon. Really I feel sorry for him because he has inherited a lot of his troubles from his predecessor.
Now, I think we have to admit this-that the minister from each province is responsible for the estimates which are allocated to that province. In other words the Minister of Health is the direct representative in the cabinet from British Columbia, and when he takes part in the cabinet councils, or when he makes his recommendations to the Minister of Finance or to the Minister of Public Works, the only conclusion is that those recommendations will be accepted. Therefore we are forced to assume that in this case the minister was either exercising his political prejudices or the government does not pay very much attention to him.
There is' a very marked difference between the estimates brought down right on the eve of an election, and estimates brought down after an election is over and the government feel safe. We have a fair illustration of that in connection with the estimates from the prairie provinces. I want to emphasize that statement from the circumstances connected with one of the cities in my own district. You all remember the general election which took place on the 29th October, 1925. With the object of giving a little prestige to my opponent -the Minister of Health purchased a site in the town of Trail for a public building. For that site, consisting of two bare lots, he paid $11,000. Of course they bought these lots from the local Liberal whip. He was the man who put the deal through. Eleven thousand dollars for two bare lots!
How much were they worth?

They were assessed at $2,300. At the other end of the same identical block there were two lots on which there was a building. The government had an option on these two lots and that building for $9,000, but they were owned by a Conservative and so their purchase was not considered. The government had a chance to purchase for $9,000 a piece of property which had a rental value of $125 per month. Yet they passed that up and purchased two vacant lots with no rental value at all for $11,000. The simple explanation of that is the influence exercised by the Minister of Health. Having purchased
1144	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-British Columbia
this site for a public building one would have supposed there would have been some intimation on the part of the Minister of Health that the construction of the building would be proceeded with. He got the lots in September, 1925. Remember, the election took place on the 29th of October, 1925. On the 4th of September, 1925, the option was exercised, and on the 27th of September, 1925, just exactly one month prior to the election, there went to the surveyor a rush wire from the resident architect in Victoria. Just to show you the political influence behind it, I may say that this rush wire said:
Will be glad if you will proceed to Trail and have a survey made with the utmost despatch as the matter is very urgent.
The utmost despatch on the eve of this election! They wanted to have this survey made.
Who sent the telegram?

It is signed by the architect of the Public Works department resident in Victoria, who of course gets his instructions from Ottawa. The Minister of Public Works at that time was the hon. gentleman who now occupies the portfolio of Health. Not satisfied, they got the lots surveyed, and for this purpose they thought it necessary to bring a naan from the outside. There are three local surveyors in the city of Trail fully qualified for any work of this nature, but instead of securing one of these men the department, simply because they were Conservatives, went to the city of Nelson fifty miles away and brought in a Liberal surveyor, whom they had to pay more than would have been charged by any of the others. They had to pay two or three days' hotel expenses for this man with the result that it cost them $50 to survey two little lots 25 by 100. I do not at all blame the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) because he must either accept or reject the recommendations of his colleague from British Columbia, and in this case I take it for granted that the latter hon. gentleman recommended what was done.
What I want to impress upon the government is this, that in five years the city of Trail has contributed to the public treasury by way of post office receipts and customs the sum of $300,000.

May I point out to
the hon. member that, according to section 5 of rule 13, speeches in committee of the whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration. Considerable

Before you rule on the
point Mr. Chairman-

that they are. We are discussing vote No. 141 which embraces items in connection with public buildings in British Columbia generally. During the last two or
three days we have been discussing votes for every other province and the widest latitude has been allowed, as is in keeping with the practice in this parliament; and I submit, Mr. Chairman, that it would be exceedingly unfair were you to rule the hon. member out of order. Mr. STEVENiS: I protest against any suggestion that time has been wasted.

speechtext:
We are agreeing with
you.

allow the chairman to say that we have been wasting time.
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: LIow can my hon. friend address that remark to the government in view of the statement I have just made, that we are willing to let the hon. gentleman proceed?
I am addressing the chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You spoke of the government.
You may as well have an understanding now as any other time.

Mr. Chairman, I would confine myself to the item, but the trouble is that it is not there; I cannot speak to it.
I was pointing out that in this particular place, the city of Trail, which I represent, nothing has been spent in the construction of public buildings, although we contribute to the federal exchequer every year four times the total vote for public buildings in British Columbia. Here is a little community of 8,000 which contributes to the treasury $1,000,000 per annum in taxation, yet the accommodation in public
buildings which it so badly needs is not given. Notwithstanding that large contribution we make to the Dominion exchequer not one dollar has been spent in public works in that city in the whole period of thirty years I have lived there. Surely, therefore, we are not extravagant in asking now for a vote for a public building.
I would point out also wherein the Dominion is indebted to Trail. Let me take you back to January, 1915. At that time the allies needed zinc, and they were being held up by a syndicate of New York brokers who were charging them forty-four cents per pound for that commodity. The city of Trail then set its research department to work with the result that it evolved a process for treating complex ores which relieved not only this government, but all the allies, for Trail was able to supply zinc at the rate of fifteen cents per pound. Should not such an accomplishment receive some consideration? To-day we are producing in this little community, which the Minister of Health would overlook, 6 per cent of the world's zinc supply and 8 per cent of its lead supply. We have there the largest industrial institution probably in the whole Dominion, except perhaps the British Empire Steel Corporation. Figured in dollars and cents our production is $35,000,000 per year, and that is one little community of 8,000 people, and yet the Minister of Health does not think it is of sufficient importance to recommend a public building to the Public Works department. We produce pure gold, pure silver, pure lead, pure copper, pure zinc, sulphuric acid, antimony and innumerable byproducts.
But you do not produce any Liberals there.

That is quite right. The
Minister of Public Works this afternoon, in attempting to justify a certain vote, said that there had been an increase in the population of the place. The community I speak for, has in five years time increased its population from 3,000 to 8,000, or an increase of
5,000	people. In that community we have a memorial hall built by the citizens themselves with the assistance of the company, and its equipment is not surpassed in the whole Dominion. It has a gymnasium, recreation rooms, bowling alleys and so forth. We have also a hospital which is the last word in construction and equipment.
I want to say a word now as to the human touch that exists as between the company and its employees. First, this company gives its men group insurance. It has also put aside
1146	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-British Columbia
several hundred thousand dollars for a pension fund, so that a man as soon as he has put in so many years with the company will be able to retire on pension. It also helps its employees in the building of homes. It has loaned to the people of this community half a million dollars for that purpose, and any man who can pay twenty per cent of the cost of his home is advanced the other eighty per cent by the company, at a very low rate of interest. With half a million dollars advanced to this community to help in the construction of homes, the Minister of Health still does not think it is of sufficient importance to give them a small public building, notwithstanding the fact that we have not had one dollar of public expenditure in thirty years. The company also gives the men in its employ fifty dollars in cash at Christmas time, and every married man who has been in the service of the company for three years gets a share of stock in the company, worth $250. The company comes just about as near looking after the welfare of its employees as it is humanly possible for any company to do It has a payroll of about $500,000 a month.
This afternoon the Minister of Public Works in justifying some of his estimates, said, "I am endeavouring to carry out a policy of constructing public buildings where there is not adequate accommodation, and where the necessity is urgent." I propose to put my case up to the hon. Minister of Public Works, and to show that the necessity for a public building in this community is urgent. I want first to read a letter from the hon. Minister of Health, who is British Columbia's direct representative in the cabinet. I had asked him to give consideration to this matter of the construction of a public building, and he replied under date of February 3, which is not very long ago:	'	1
I am thoroughly conversant with the necessities of that district-
Meaning my district:
-and it was with a view to giving better accommodation that I recommended the purchase of a property in Trail some time ago-
That "some time ago" was just a month before the 1925 election:
-it being my intention to advocate the erection of a suitable building on this site.
Now I would ask the present Minister of Public Works if the former Minister of Public Works, who is now the Minister of Health, advocated a vote for this building. He says further:
I am sure it is the desire of the government to meet the requirements of the fast-growing
[Mr. Esling.l
communities in Canada, but it is well realized that owing to the Great war there was a general desire to curtail public expenditure. It is only within the last two or three years that the government has been able to see its way clear to undertake the construction of new buildings, some of which have been completed.
The Minister of Health apparently has not seen his way clear to recommend the construction of this urgently needed building.
Now I want to quote from a letter from the present Postmaster General. I put this matter up to him, and he was very sympathetic. He did not merely say: I will give it consideration. No, under date of January 4, he wrote:
I may say that the construction of public buildings is a matter of policy resting with the Minister of Public Works, but I have already made representations to his department that the accommodation at present provided at Trail is totally inadequate, and have urged the erection of a suitable public building.
That comes direct from the Postmaster General himself

"the accommodation is totally inadequate, and have urged the erection of a suitable public building." I have given you the letter from the Minister of Health, showing that he realizes the necessity for this public building in Trail; I have given you the letter from the Postmaster General, saying that he 'has urged the Department of Public Works to construct a building in Trail. Now I want to quote from the Post Office department itself. The conditions in the city of Trail became so acute, and are so acute to-day, that the Post Office department sent a special inspector to Trail to investigate the conditions, and this inspector reported:
The present quarters cover 1,218 feet of floor space.
The building Which the government rejected contains something like 1,500 feet of floor space. The inspector also reported that there were 1,037 boxes, and that the postmaster there stated that there were 500 people waiting to get boxes. That is, there were 1,037 boxes in use, and 500 people were lined up there waiting to get boxes. There is only room in that post office for 100 boxes, and the postmaster hesitates to put them in, because he has to put them in at his own expense, and he fears that if he did so, the government might construct a public building, and he would be out the cost of the hundred boxes. The inspector further goes on to say that the congestion in Trail has been so great that it has been necessary, in order to accommodate the general public, to establish four places throughout the city where the public can purchase stamps. Trail to-day, he

Supply-Public Works-British Columbia
says, has a population of 8,000, and he believes that it will increase in three years to probably
12,000.	That is what the post office inspector says, the man who went into this community to make a full investigation of the conditions, and he naturally went to the fountainhead for information; in other words, to the company.

Will the hon. gentleman
give the date of that report?

I cannot give you the date, but I can give you the month. The report was made in December, 1926, only a short time ago. He say's that within three years that community will have a population of 12,000. If you were to go to the manager of the Consolidated Mining & Smelting Company, I am sure he would hazard the guess that Trail will have a population of 15,000 souls within the next four or five years. This report from the inspector is in the possession of the Postmaster General and I have no doubt that upon it he based his recommendation to the Minister of Public Works. The government's own inspector recommends the erection of a public building to be proceeded with as soon as possible. He further recommends that this building, instead of containing 1,037 letter boxes should contain 2,100 letter boxes. Surely any hon. member who wants to be fair about this matter will realize that it is a case of urgency, or inadequate accommodation and of necessity. The inspector recommends that instead of 1,200 square feet of floor space as at present, the building should have 3,500 feet of floor space, and in order to avoid congestion, he also urges that there should be two entrances.
There is not another industrial centre in the whole of Canada to equal the city of Trail. In that city, an, amount of $1,000,000 is paid each year in taxes and we have not had one dollar spent for public works in thirty years except the $11,000 vote which the minister passed on to his Liberal whip for that site. From my short acquaintance with the present Minister of Public Works I believe he is disposed to be fair. I do not blame him a particle; I put all the responsibility on the minister from British Columbia who apparently has not made the recommendation. I am simply going to leave the matter there and ask for the good offices and fair consideration of the present minister. I will ask him if he will not realize the lack of accommodation in the city of Trail, and endeavour to bring down in the supplementary estimates a vote for the erection of a public building there. At the present time the government are spending $135 a month in rent, $100 for a post office
and $35 for a customs house. They might just as well save that money and house the two departments in one building. If the former Minister of Public Works saw the necessity, urgency and rush for getting this post office site purchased from his local Liberal friend before the 29th day of October, the date of the 1925 election, surely the sitting member is justified in asking for a vote for the erection of a public building in Trail.

I am rather surprised and grieved to find my hon. friend in such an irritable mood to-night. He complains very bitterly of my action as the minister from British Columbia. I think the fact that as the minister knowing conditions in Trail and knowing them as well as my hon. friend does, I purchased the property which he says I purchased from Liberal friends-
From the Liberal whip, I said.
I am advised that my hon. friend and some of his real estate associates in Trail were anxious to sell a site.
I rise to a point of order.
My hon. friend has been talking for about an hour about a post office in Trail-

Will the minister confine
himself to the truth.

I am going to
speak for five minutes. The purchase of the property was done through the ordinary channels.
On the minister's order.
Is it possible for my hon. friend to contain himself? I know he has not got over the fact that the people of Trail did not give him a majority in the last election.
They did. They gave me a majority of fifteen against your friend you brought from five hundred miles away.
I wish to say this because my hon. friend has gone far out of his way to intimate that I personally purchased property in Trail.
So the minister did.

My hon. friend
will retract that statement, because it is not true. I will wait for him to retract.

I will not say that the minister went there and handed over the money. I will say that he sent his resident architect and told him to s >e a certain man.
I14s	COMMONS
Supply-Public Works-British Columbia

It is easy for anyone to make insinuations, but this property was bought by the Public Works department in the usual way and any hon. member can easily inform himself upon the procedure that was followed. An officer of the department goes to the town or place where the purchase is to be made; he makes inquiries; he examines different properties.
He did not. He was told to see a certain man and he saw him. He was told to see the Liberal whip and he saw him.
He inquired as to values of many properties.
He saw just the one man.
I do not quite appreciate my hon. friend's attitude. I think I am entitled to speak for a few moments.
Well, speak the truth.

When my hon. friend had the floor I did not interrupt him, and I would ask him to contain himself and suggest that he have papers brought down as they were last year giving the details of that purchase.
I have them under my hand; every one of them.

If the hon. member will read the report of the engineers, I am sure he will realize that he has been labouring for an hour in vain and has not been representing the true facts or conditions in regard to the matter. I was pleased to have my hon. friend endorse a vote of $5,000 for Kimberley. I can well understand that, because the great Sullivan mine is there. The town of Trail would not be the town it is to-day if the mine at Kimberley was not in operation. There is no doubt that Trail is a fine industrial community, and it is my hope and desire that money will be provided whereby proper government offices will be erected for the advantage of the people of Trail.
It needs them as much as Kensington, Prince Edward Island, does.
I will ask him if it needs them as much as the people of Prince Rupert do, and I will then ask him to dilate on the purchase of a site in Prince Rupert, giving the date and the price paid for it.

The minister might add
the Prince Rupert elevator.
It is serving a useful purpose.

Returning $100 a year
to this government on an investment of $1,500,000.

I do not wish to continue, because it is not necessary, but I take exception to the desire of my hon. friend to make a speech in this House for the purpose of making a little political capital for himself by attacking me.

I have the very report
about which the minister speaks from the resident architect at Victoria. I will leave it to any three members on the other side of the House who know anything about building construction, and I know they will pronounce it the most absurd, ridiculous and unjust report that was ever made on a public building site.

I am not interested in the
Trail post office; I am not interested even in a public building at Kimberley, but I am interested in the lack of public buildings in the district of Comox-Alberni. I would like to call the attention of this committee, and more particularly of my Conservative friends, to the fact that this vote comprises the sum of $243,262, and with the exception of the small sum of $5,000 for Kimberley the whole of that sum is for buildings in districts represented by Conservatives. Except, I say, for that little vote of $5,000 for Kimberley, every one of the twelve votes is going to districts of hon. gentlemen opposite, one of whom has made so much complaint of how he and his Conservative friends in British Columbia have been treated. I hope the lesson will be taken to heart by them, and that when I ask the Minister of Public Works for some few niggardly votes for odd wharves later on, hon. gentlemen opposite will remember this vote.
It is pretty hard to find anything but a Conservative out there.
Conditions might be improved, though.
How many patients are there at this lazaretto?
Last year there were seven.

The same number both
years.

From what parts do they come?
As far as I recall, one is from Saskatchewan, and four are Chinamen. Fortunately the number of lepers is decreasing at all our stations.

Item agreed to.
British Columbia-Dominion public buildings -improvements, repairs, etc., $40,000.

So much has been said regarding certain places where post offices are to be built that their names have become historic during the last few days. Let me mention another place that has not a post office building-the large, thriving city of Prince Rupert. The postal and other government business is carried on in a rented building costing annually about $4,000. The postal revenue for 1926 was $35,439; the customs and excise, $301,480. Besides these services the Marine and Fisheries department and the government telegraph department have accommodation in the same building. But it is not by any means adequate for the purpose. One of the government's representatives from Victoria visited Prince Rupert while I wias there and after going through the building expressed the opinion that it was neither hygienic nor suitable for the amount of business handled. I do not expect that I shall be able to induce the government to promise me a post office to-night, but undoubtedly they should consider the desirability even from the standpoint of economy alone, of erecting a building at Prince Rupert adequate to handle the large volume of government business that has to be transacted there, rather than pay out every year $4,000 in rent for undesirable accommodation. In Smithers, a very promising town, the postal revenue for 1926 was $4,854, and at Ocean Falls, $6,596. I think since other places have had so many successful advocates, Prince Rupert and those I have just mentioned are entitled to favourable consideration from the government.

Could the Minister of Public Works tell us how many troops are stationed in Esquimalt?

Item agreed to.
William Head quarantine station-repairs and improvements, $8,250.

I would like to ask the
Postmaster General if he has had any report in regard to the necessity of a post office building in the town of Prince George?
From memory I would say not, but there may be an application on file. I will look it up and let my hon. friend know.

I would point out the
necessity of recommending to the Minister of Public Works an amount for a public building in the town of Prince George. That town is a very important community in the central part of British Columbia, with a population of about 3,500 people, and last year the postal revenue amounted to $12,412. I notice that in the estimates many places are receiving substantial consideration from this government which have neither the revenue nor the population of Prince George. I asked that this be included in the estimates last year and it was not done; I ask again that in view of the development likely to take place in the course of the next year, consideration be given to this request by the Minister of Public Works and the postal authorities. There is also an inspector of customs at that point, and! a very considerable revenue is derived in that way. There is also in my district the town of Salmon Arm, with a population of between 1,200 and 1,500, which produces a postal revenue of about $8,800. In addition to the postal and customs revenue at this point I would point out that there are officials of the Forestry branch of the Interior department stationed in that town, and the rentals paid for office quarters must be very considerable. I suggest that it would be in the interests of the government and would reduce expenditure by a very considerable amount to erect a public building of their own in that town and thereby give the necessary accommodation to the various officials stationed there. There is not an item in the estimates for either of these places, but I am hoping the minister will be good enough to include them when the supplementary estimates are prepared. The Minister of Health (Mr. King) laughs; perhaps he remembers that last year he promised to do this for me, and to give it his very serious consideration. He is still considering, but I hope he will pass along a favourable decision this year.

I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if it is the intention of the government to give northern British Columbia an experimental farm?
If it is the intention of the government to give my hon. friend a farm?

No, not to me, to northern
British Columbia.

The estimates of
the Department of Agriculture will be up after a while, and I will be able then to give my hon. friend all the information he desires.

This is a very important
question for the mixed farming districts of the Buckley valley, Bums lake, Smithers, Telkwa, Francois lake and Ootsa lake. Some years ago this question was before the House and was favourably considered by the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). I think that it would be a very intelligent method of expenditure, because the result of the establishment of an experimental farm in this particular district would be far reaching. This district is one of the most suitable and best adapted to mixed farming in Canada, and the people of that great district which includes thousands of square miles are engaged in ail forms of agricultural industry. They have splendid root crops; they carry on dairying; they have wheat, oats, rye, and timothy, and every other crop which should encourage the government to give these people an experimental farm. The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Toimie) some years ago very strongly advocated an experimental farm for this particular part of British Columbia, and I believe the time has now come in this country when the question of mixed farming should receive more careful consideration. We have the great wheat fields of the prairie provinces, but we must consider the other great, districts of Canada which are perfectly adapted to mixed farming, and the district to which I refer should have an experimental farm, and the government should assist what is recognized to be a substantitl forward movement in the development of a great industry. When I heard the number of advocates for public buildings I was not enthusiastic, but I do feel that when the question is one of national importance, concerning the well-being of 
Canada, the voice of these people should be heard and the government Should be sympathetic. I trust, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Agriculture is of the same mind to-day as he was in 1924.

Would the minister explain
on what farms and what buildings this money is to be spent?

This is for replacements,
improvements, alterations, repairs and so forth on the various experimental farms and stations throughout the Dominion.

I understand it is all

Is that all for buildings
in Ottawa?

I think tlhe amount for

Is it the intention of the
government to proceed with the erection of new departmental buildings, and thus reduce the expenditure for rents?

It is expected that the first will be commenced this year and that it will take a couple of years to complete. We shall not be relieved of any rental until the new building is habitable.

Has it been decided what
departments will be housed in the new building?

Has the department any
complete plan in regard to the buildings contemplated? *
We had a plan prepared some time ago, providing for a complete set of departmental buildings sufficient to house the various departments. The scheme is rather extensive.
What is the total cost?

Does that include
public buildings for all departments?

No, only by provinces. We have 402 buildings rented at a total of $1,-
440,000.

In London, England, we have an expenditure of $9,733.30; Nova Scotia, $11,010; Prince Edward Island, $811; New Brunswick, $11,922; Quebec, $97,658; Ontario, $168,980; Ottawa, $650,377; Manitoba, $67,059; Saskatchewan, $76,156; Alberta, $143,868; British Columbia, $65,725; Yukon, $660; militia probable requirements, $34,660; militia rents, pending, $10,931; militia colleges and universities, $20,000,

high commissioner and other officials.

We have already been given an item of $660 for Yukon. What does this item include?

This is required for repairs, fuel, lighting, water service, and salary of caretakers in. connection with public buildings occupied by government officials in the Yukon Territory during the fiscal year 1927-28.

What does the
