Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers-Nova Scotia, $296,210. Mr. SMITH (Cumberland): Will the minister explain the first item of $1,850 for repairs to the dyke at Amherst Point?

This is a dyke in the county of Cumberland. It is proposed to rebuild it on a length of 190 feet. To carry out the proposed repairs, it will be necessary to drive a line of piles along the outer face of the work and lay planking on the inner side of these piles to hold the back filling of the dyke. It is also suggested that anchor piles be driven about ten feet in from the outer face of the dyke and suitable braces placed from these piles to the top of the piles along the outer face, to give stability to the works.
Do I understand that these repairs are to protect the government wharf at Amherst Point?

Yes. The dyke west of
the public road at the government wharf is badly in need of repairs and the. farmers' body who own the land in this vicinity have asked the department to undertake these repairs.

The wharf
itself is in a dilapidated condition. Last year a small sum was spent on it, but I believe it was used largely to dig berths to enable vessels to discharge their cargoes there.
That would be dredging.

Yes; a small
amount was spent for that purpose. The wharf itself has been in disuse for a considerable time, but the people are now beginning to make use of it and, temporary repairs having been effected, cargoes have been landed. Representations have been made to me that the flooring on the wharf is not only out of repair but unsafe, and I understand that the board of trade of the town, which is about two miles from the wharf, have asked the department to have the necessary work done so that cargoes may be properly and safely discharged at this point. Has the minister taken these representations into consideration?

The position in regard to wharves is much the same as in regard to public buildings. We have in the Dominion of Canada to-day 2,147 wharves of various kinds. The number was a great surprise to me when I was going over the list with a view to seeing on which ones repairs were most urgently needed. My hon. friend will recall that in the last thirteen years, since the outbreak of the war, there has not been anything like the expenditure on wharves that the people in the various localities thought was necessary, and the result has been that many of them have fallen exactly into the condition that I have no doubt my hon. friend finds this one in. We are trying to make repairs where they are most urgently required, and not to go beyond the amount of money that the government can afford to spend, and we are aiming to make these repairs as far as passible in places where they will encourage production and the distribution of the wealth created in that particular part of the Dominion. I quite agree with my hon. friend that that wharf and many others must be repaired just as soon as funds can be found to do it.

That is all very nice, but these are public services, and from that standpoint alone they should be maintained in order to provide the public with the

Sup-ply-Harbours and Rivers-N.S.
accommodation that is required. But leaving that out of consideration for the moment, there is still another viewpoint, and that is the question of what is economy in the long run. If these services are allowed to go into decay, in the end the cost of putting them into proper condition will far exceed any outlay that would have to be made in the interim and the repairs will serve two purposes, namely, save money and provide adequate service. I wish to speak also of other services of a similar character in the county of Cumberland, the same county in which this Amherst Point dyke expenditure is to be made. I would refer the minister to the breakwater and beach protection at a point called Port Greville. A breakwater was constructed there about a couple of years ago, but it was built a considerable distance short of the old one. It was built to protect the harbour and to stop the filling in of the channel of the river on account of tides moving back and forth. Representations have been made to the government to extend this breakwater out to the point where the old one was, in an endeavour to stop the filling in of the channel. It has also been pointed out to me and to the government that the breakwater itself has not been completely constructed, and in order to afford proper harbour protection the breakwater will have to be thoroughly spiled, which is not the case to-day. This is a very important port on the bay of Fundy. Last year there was shipped through it 5,000,000 feet of lumber. There were 31 three and four masted schooners repaired there; 14 large vessels cleared with lumber, there were 8 cargoes of piling, and 16 cargoes of lumber in smaller vessels, also
1,000,000 feet of lumber shipped in scows. In all over 30,000 tons deadweight was shipped out of this hatbour last year.
What was the value?

I have not
the value in dollars, just the quantities, but it is recognized that this is a most important port.

Is not this a wharf on
which considerable expenditure has been made by the government in the last two years?
Yes, considerable expenditures have been made on the breakwater, but nothing on the beach protection.
About $50,000 in the last .two years.

I do not think that much; but the work has not been finished. The breakwater to-day is not completed; the beach protection is practically useless, and on account of that fact it is not rendering the service to this port that it should. Last year, or the year before, private interests had to dig the channel out in order to allow their large vessels to enter and clear. I understand also that the citizens of that port have made representations to the government for consideration. Certainly I did myself last year and also this year.
I pass now just as quickly as possible to another point on the bay of Fundy. At Spencer's island there is a wharf which is in a dilapidated condition, and for which no provision is made in the estimates. I have before me a communication from the Public Works department in Halifax, which I presume is a branch of the Public Works department here, stating that they were going to ask that the sum of $2,000 be placed in this year's estimates in order to put this wharf in repair. This is also an important point, but I find nothing in the estimates to provide for this work. The matter is one that should certainly be given some consideration by the minister when the supplementary estimates are brought down.
Then at West Advocate there is a breakwater, and the people there are asking for an extension. This is also a very important port through which a great deal of lumber and other commodities are shipped. I am taking these matters up only very briefly, and am not going into details at all, although I have here very valuable information; but I do not wish to delay the committee. I would ask the minister if there will not be some reconsideration in the supplementary estimates of the amounts allotted for harbours and rivers in Nova Scotia,, particularly in Cumberland county at the ports to which I have made reference to-night. I believe that in the end economy will be effected by the immediate repairing of these public works, instead of allowing them to go on for a number of years more without attention, when the cost of repairs will be excessive.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the desire of the committee to take up this vote item by item? The amounts are comparatively small, and perhaps we could have a general discussion on the resolution.
Item by item.

I want to point out to the Minister of Public Works that in the supplementary estimates for 1926-27 there were five



Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.S.
items affecting my constituency, as follows: Brooklyn wharf repairs, $1,500; La Have river, dredging, $35,000; Pentz wharf, $4,400; Port Mouton dredging, $55,500; and West Port Joli, breakwater repairs, $3,800. Since the supplementary estimates were brought down not one dollar of that money, so far as I can ascertain, has -been expended; in other words the vote will lapse and nothing will have been done by the 31st of March. In the main estimates tabled this year not one of these items has been reinstated-, although I note that fifteen other items in the supplementaries for 1926-27 have been carried into the main estimates for the present year. I would like to ask the minister why the five items I have mentioned have been dropped. The whole five of them are in my constituency. None of them has been included and I want to point out further that I -have drawn the attention of his department to the fact that the wharf at Tancook is in a bad state of repair; that the breakwater at Blandford is in a bad state of repair; that the wharf at Vogler's cove is in the same condition, and additional dredging is required at Port Mouton. I am going to ask the minister again if he will be kind enough to give these matters his attention and provide for them in the supplementary estimates this year. Every one of them is a service which is urgent and important to the locality.

Just to continue the argument of the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Ernst), I might also refer to the supplementary estimates of a year ago. As regards the constituency which I have the honour to represent, a year ago we had an item of $1,000 for repairs to a wharf and road at Chezzetcook (Murphy's or Myatt's). Then there was another item of $4,800 for a wharf at Ketch harbour and an item of $3,500 for wharf at Necum Teuch. I notice in the estimates for this year an item for wharf repairs at Musquodoboit, $1,600. I have no criticism of that item whatever; I wish it were a little larger, because Musquodoboit wias particularly good to me in 1926. There is an item for dredging at Sheet harbour. That is also absolutely necessary and I do not see how * the government can get away from doing the work. There is an item for $1,100 for breakwater repairs and improvements at Devil's island. This is absolutely necessary and I thought the vote would be larger. Devil's island is an island at the mouth of the western entrance of Halifax harbour and on it are situated two very important lighthouses. There is also a life-
saving station and there is no telephone connection. A cable can be run across the eastern passage a very short distance and I would ask, not only in the interests of the residents of that island but as a necessary work in connection with the life-saving station, that there should be a telephone connection between that island and the city of Halifax or the town of Dartmouth.
What is the distance?
Not more than a quarter of a mile.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister some much needed improvements in my constituency. There is the port of Westport in Digby county, one of the most important fishing ports in that county. A breakwater was built some years ago at a-cost of $75,000 or $100,000, and to-day it requires an extension of about 50 to 75 feet owing to the fact that it was not properly dredged out by the department and the port cannot be use-d at low tide. There is a recommendation to the Department of Public Works from the Department of Trade and Commerce stating that this work is urgently required, but there is nothing in the estimates for it. A great deal of dredging is needed at a number of the piers and breakwaters in my -constituency. Part of my constituency is a fishing district and perhaps there are more breakwaters in it than in any other constituency in Nova Scotia. I would urge upon the minister the necessity of making improvements to a number of these, including Westport; Battery point; dredging at the Rac-quette at Digby harbour; Anderson's cove and Litchfield. All of these are very urgently needed in order to give proper facilities for oa,Trying on the fishing industry in those places. I would urge -the minister to have his engineers report on these places and to have a sufficient amount placed in the supplementary estimates to carry out this urgently required work.

I know that in regard to
some of the places mentioned by my hon. friend, and at least one of the places mentioned by the hon. member for Cumberland, the engineer has been asked to make a report. That does not necessarily mean that an amount will be placed in -the estimates -this year, but I can assure my hon. friend that the matter of supplementary estimates, which must of -course depend upon the amount of money that we h-ave at our disposal, is receiving the greatest possible attention. I am quite satisfied, and I -think I should not

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.S.
withhold the statement from my hon. friends, now that only a small number of the requests made in regard to places throughout the whole country can be acceded to with the money at hand. On account very largely of the fact that there seems to be a revival of optimism and of business prosperity at every harbour in the country, the demands have been much greater in the last year or so than ever before. I recall a number of the places that have been mentioned to-night. There is no question that some of the breakwaters are in quite serious condition. There are several other places w'here, on account of new developments such as pulp and paper and other industries, it is necessary, if you are to encourage those industries, that something be done. It is wholly a question of making such improvements as our finances will permit and such as are necessary in order to assist the general production and prosperity of the community concerned.

That is a very fair statement if the minister would only carry it out. The fact is that money is not expended where it is most urgently needed. If the minister would carry out the principle that he has laid down, that would be satisfactory to all of us on this side of the House. As regards all the places I have mentioned, the improvements are urgently needed. The government have expended hundreds of thousands of dollars on breakwaters throughout the different counties in Nova Scotia. Why do they not keep them in repair just the same as a private individual keeps his wharves in repair? The trouble is that in certain localities the government allow these wharves to go down, for some reason that is unexplained. That is not good policy, because if you do not make repairs when necessary, if you allow these works to go without repair for another year, you have eventually to spend double the money. The engineers know what is required. It would be satisfactory if the government would carry out their recommendations, but they are not carried out. The money is spent often where it is not needed and places where it is needed have to go without.
There is an item of $2,500 for breakwater repairs at Black Point. Where is that situated in Nova Scotia?

In the constituency of
Richmond-West Cape Breton.
I notice for Black Point the vote is $2,500 and last year it was $1,400. How much of that $1,400 was spent?

What
was that expended for?

For sealing up the outer
end of the work done in 1925-26, and placing ballast in two bays on the seaward side and repairing the sheathing at those bays.

If the
breakwater was repaired in 1925 why this vote for $2,500 now?

Does my hon. friend
object to the expenditure?
No, but I want to see where the money is going.

The vote is for the reconstruction of the outer sixty feet of the breakwater, sixty feet by eighteen by eighteen, with native timber cribwork. This reconstruction started in 1925-26, when seventy-five feet of the 110 feet proposed was built. The work was stopped on account of stormy weather. Twenty-five feet of the outer end was destroyed in the fall of 1925-26 by storms. The estimated cost of the work proposed for 192728 is $2,500.

How
much was expended previous to the general election in 1925? I understand the work was stopped in October.

My statement shows the
expenditure last year.

You
have no statement of the money expended up to October 1925?
No.

Apparently it has become necessary to vote $2,500 to repair the part that was left unfinished just a few days after the election. That breakwater was built around 1911 or 1912. The money for it had been voted previous to the 1911 election, for under the patronage system of our friends they always voted money for such projects the year before a general election. A certain amount of money was spent in the district previous to 1911. Before that time some work had been done at the entrance to the Grand1 river against the best advice of the fishermen in the district. Due to this work and the construction of the breakwater the entrance to the river was closed by shifting sand and fishermen cannot fish in that district. Now we are proposing to spend another $2,500 after having already spent five or six thousand dollars in 1925, on work that has been destroyed, for you cannot hold the breakwater in that position. As I say, the portion of the breakwater still re-

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.S.
maining is helping to block the entrance to the Grand river, so that to-day we are left practically without a fishing port in that district. I would urge that the department send a competent engineer to survey the locality and ascertain if it is not feasible to keep open the Grand river by a little dredging and the construction of abutments. I understood that the people in the district were to forward a petition to the government asking that this be done. By clearing the channels at the entrance to the Grand river the government would open up one of the finest pulpwood areas left in Cape Breton, an area which is along the river, and which communicates with four large lakes. I would strongly urge that this be done not only for the development of the Grand river as a fishing port but also for the development of the pulp industry in that district.
I have before me the report of the district engineer, Mr. Locke, whom I take to be a competent official. I assume my hon. friend does not suggest that the local engineer is not competent?

The local engineer in that district is, I understand, a very competent man. In 1925 the people of that district asked the government to inspect this region and report on the feasibility of reopening the Grand river. I think Mr. Locke, if so instructed, would be able to present to the government a very favourable report, and for a little expenditure we would have that district developed to its fullest extent. The government should guard1 against this $2,500 on the Black Point breakwater being wasted. Black Point is just across the entrance of the Grand river.
I also notice that the item for dredging at Petite de Grat harbour is omitted. What has become of the $30,000 that was voted for this previous to the election in 1925?

My reports cover only
the details of the items in the estimates.

Mr. Chairman, is not the minister aware that $30,000 was voted for the dredging of Petite de Gra-t harbour in 1925? The work was let to a, certain contractor, but after a few weeks the dredging was stopped. It is a very important public work but it has been neglected by this government ever since.

I do not think my hon.
friend would expect me to carry information in my head in regard to all these items. I have the file in the office relating to this [Mr. F. MacDonald.!
particular matter and I shall be glad to obtain whatever information there is and give it to my hon. friend.

I do
not expect the minister to carry all the information in his cranium, but I would expect that with his deputy at his beck and call and with all the files of the department available he would have some knowledge at least of such an important contract. I would suggest to the minister that in the supplementary estimates the remaining portion of that $30,000 be included, which will open up that important port and permit the fishing industry to continue. This is probably the only industry the people in that district have; it is a fresh fish industry and these people are about the nearest to the best winter fishing in Nova Scotia. There are some twenty-five or thirty boats fishing out of that port and the haddock winter fishing is very important there. This money was voted in 1925 but work was stopped in October of that year and there has not been a stroke of work done since. I would suggest that the remaining portion of that money be revoted in order to permit work to commence at once. Have contractors who should be able to carry out any contracts they enter into, and if they do not do so it is the business of the government to see that the work is carried on or the contract forfeited.
I would also like to bring to the attention of the minister another matter in connection with the Fourchu district; I notice there is an amount included in the estimates for repairs to beach for the protection of that harbour. These repairs were made in 1925; the work was done under foremen appointed by this government; it was used for patronage purposes, and within two weeks of its completion every dollar's worth of work was washed away. If we are now going to spend more money on this project we should at least see that it is spent properly and that proper materials are used so that it will withstand the weather.
I would also bring to the attention of the minister the question of a life saving station at Scatterie island. I understand that a life saving station was established there some years ago, but during the last few years this government allowed it to be closed; it was stated they would not pay their men a reasonable salary. I do not know what the reason was; it was not that they did not vote right, because up until 1925 Scatterie island always gave a good strong Liberal majority, but in 1926 it did not do so because they felt that they were neglected.
